Proposal for OPA1 Overexpression (AAV-OPA1)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Nature and origin: The candidate is a gene‐therapy construct encoding human OPA1 (optic atrophy 1), packaged in an engineered adeno‐associated virus (AAV) vector, most often an AAV2/8 or AAV2/7 chimera known to transduce retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) efficiently after subretinal injection. OPA1 is an endogenous mitochondrial inner‐membrane‐localized dynamin‐related GTPase. The coding sequence is cloned into an AAV expression cassette under the control of an RPE‐specific or ubiquitous promoter (e.g., VMD2 or CAG). Production follows standard triple‐transfection of HEK293 cells, viral harvest, iodixanol gradient purification, and titering by qPCR.  
• Therapeutic class: This belongs to the viral‐mediated gene‐therapy class, specifically monogenic gene‐augmentation therapy. Gene therapies have precedent in ocular disease: Luxturna (AAV2‐RPE65) for Leber’s congenital amaurosis, voretigene for retinal dystrophy, and multiple AAV‐based constructs in clinical trials for other inherited retinal diseases.  

Therapeutic History  
• Use of OPA1 in disease: OPA1 loss‐of‐function mutations underlie dominant optic atrophy type 1, with clinical trials exploring nucleic acid–based rescue in hereditary optic atrophy. Preclinical studies have overexpressed OPA1 via adenovirus or AAV in models of retinal ischemia, glaucoma, and chemically induced RPE injury.  
• Application in dry AMD: No registered clinical trial or approved therapy directly uses OPA1 for dry age‐related macular degeneration. However, several groups have shown that in ARPE‐19 cells, adenoviral OPA1 expression prevents H₂O₂‐induced mitochondrial depolarization, cytochrome c release, and apoptosis (Chen et al., 2017). In vivo, AAV2/8‐OPA1 delivered subretinally in mice challenged with sodium iodate (a chemical RPE‐damaging agent that mimics features of dry AMD) preserved RPE morphology and electroretinogram (ERG) responses (Wang et al., 2019).  

Mechanism of Action  
• Physiological role of OPA1: OPA1 resides in the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM) and is proteolytically processed into long (L) and short (S) forms that cooperatively regulate mitochondrial fusion of the IMM and maintain cristae architecture. Proper OPA1 levels ensure tight cristae junctions, stabilize respiratory‐chain supercomplexes, and regulate cytochrome c sequestration.  
• Molecular cascade:  
 – Overexpression increases IMM fusion, promoting a connected mitochondrial network less susceptible to fragmentation under oxidative or metabolic stress.  
 – Stabilization of cristae junctions prevents aberrant release of cytochrome c into the intermembrane space and cytosol, arresting activation of the intrinsic apoptotic cascade (Caspase‐9 → Caspase‐3).  
 – Enhanced respiratory supercomplex stability reduces electron leak, diminishing reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and preserving mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm).  
 – In RPE cells exposed to sublethal stress (e.g., H₂O₂ or NaIO₃), OPA1 overexpression restores ΔΨm (measured via JC‐1 or TMRE assays), reduces mitochondrial‐derived ROS (e.g., measured with MitoSOX or DCFDA), and lowers Annexin V/PI–positive apoptotic cell fractions.  

Expected Effect in Dry AMD Context  
• Assay readouts: In primary or immortalized human RPE cultures challenged with oxidative stressors (H₂O₂, NaIO₃) or A2E‐photooxidation, AAV‐mediated OPA1 overexpression is expected to:  
 – Maintain ΔΨm and ATP production (measured via luminescent assays, Seahorse XF analysis).  
 – Decrease ROS levels and lipid peroxidation markers (4‐HNE, MDA).  
 – Lower apoptotic indices (TUNEL, Caspase‐3 activation).  
 – Preserve tight‐junction integrity (ZO‐1 staining) and phagocytic capacity (ingestion of photoreceptor outer segments).  
• In vivo relevance: Subretinal AAV‐OPA1 should protect RPE morphology (monitored by fundus imaging, OCT, RPE flat mounts) and visual function (ERG a‐ and b‐waves) in rodent or nonhuman primate models of RPE atrophy.  
• Expression profile: Literature confirms robust expression of OPA1 mRNA and protein in human RPE (RPE65 co‐localized), and ARPE‐19 cells transduced with control AAV reporters demonstrate high transduction efficiency with AAV2/8 or AAV2/7 vectors.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
 • Strong mechanistic rationale: Mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress are central to RPE degeneration in dry AMD, and OPA1 directly targets mitochondrial dynamics and bioenergetics.  
 • Preclinical proof‐of‐concept: Published in vitro and in vivo studies demonstrate protection of RPE structure and function under AMD‐relevant stress paradigms.  
 • AAV platform maturity: Ocular gene therapy has an established safety and regulatory pathway; subretinal delivery confines the vector to the target tissue.  
Weaknesses and Challenges  
 • Heterogeneity of dry AMD: Complement dysregulation, lipid deposition (drusen), and inflammation also drive disease; OPA1 addresses principally mitochondrial injury. Combination therapy may be required.  
 • Dosage and regulation: Excessive OPA1 can hyper‐fuse mitochondria, impairing mitophagy and promoting accumulation of damaged organelles. Fine‐tuning expression levels (e.g., via tissue‐specific or inducible promoters) will be critical.  
 • Immune and safety considerations: Potential for anti‐AAV neutralizing antibodies, long‐term expression safety (insertional mutagenesis is low with AAV, but immune responses can occur), and transgene immunogenicity.  
 • Translational gaps: Sodium iodate injury is an acute model; dry AMD develops chronically with multifactorial drivers. Demonstrating benefit in more faithful animal models (e.g., aged mice with complement factor H variants) will be important.  
Conclusion  
AAV‐mediated OPA1 overexpression is a compelling mitochondrial‐targeted strategy to preserve RPE viability under oxidative stress, with encouraging preclinical data. Its success will hinge on optimized vector design and addressing the multifactorial nature of dry AMD, potentially in combination with complement modulators or anti‐inflammatory approaches. Further studies in chronic, genetically predisposed animal models and dose‐escalation safety assessments are warranted before clinical translation.

Proposal for Compstatin Analog (Cp40)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Origin and discovery  
  – Cp40 is a second-generation compstatin analogue, derived by structure-guided optimization of the original compstatin (a 13-residue cyclic peptide discovered by phage-display screening in 1996 (Sahu et al., 1996)). Iterative substitutions at positions 4, 6, 8 and the N-terminus (addition of a D-Tyr or D–Trp moiety) increased serum half-life, binding affinity (KD ~0.5–0.7 nM vs. ~1.3 µM for compstatin) and inhibitory potency (Qu et al., 2013). The resulting 14-residue cyclic peptide (Ac–I[CVVQDWGHPMWG]–NH₂ with strategic nonproteinogenic side chains) is known as Cp40 (also termed AMY-101 in some preclinical reports).  
• Class of therapeutic compounds  
  – Cp40 belongs to the compstatin family of complement inhibitors—small cyclic peptides that bind complement component C3 and prevent its proteolytic activation. Peptidomimetics in this class are being aggressively pursued as anti-inflammatory agents in a variety of complement-driven diseases (Ricklin & Lambris, 2007).  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical and clinical development  
  – Original compstatin analogues showed efficacy in primate models of sepsis, transplant rejection and periodontitis. Cp40 (AMY-101) has advanced to Phase I/II trials in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) and is under investigation for COVID-19-associated hyperinflammation (Mastellos et al., 2021).  
  – A closely related pegylated derivative, pegcetacoplan (APL-2), has completed Phase III trials for geographic atrophy (GA) secondary to dry AMD (FILLY study; Liao et al., 2020), demonstrating a ~20% reduction in GA lesion growth at 1 year (p < 0.01). Although Cp40 itself has not yet entered AMD trials, its mechanism and superior binding profile make it a strong candidate for retinal applications.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Target engagement and biochemical interactions  
  – Cp40 binds with high affinity to the beta-chain of human C3 in the region of the macroglobulin (MG) domains 4 and 5, sterically occluding the C3 convertase cleavage site (C3bBb) and thus preventing generation of both C3a/C3b and downstream C5 convertase activity (Janssen et al., 2007).  
  – By halting C3 activation, Cp40 blocks opsonization, anaphylatoxin release (C3a, C5a) and assembly of the membrane attack complex (MAC, C5b-9).  
• Molecular consequences in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)  
  – Sub-lytic MAC deposition on RPE induces Ca²⁺ influx, mitochondrial depolarization (ΔΨm loss) and production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-6, IL-1β) (Ferrington et al., 2016). Cp40’s blockade of C3 impairs formation of C5b, thereby reducing C5b-9 assembly and sub-lytic stress on RPE cells.  
  – ARPE-19 cells express complement components (C3, factor B), receptors (CD46/MCP, CD55/DAF, CD59) and regulatory proteins, making them a valid in vitro model for complement-mediated injury (Li et al., 2009).  

Expected Effect in Proposed Assay  
• Reduction of sub-lytic MAC on ARPE-19  
  – In published assays, 1 µM Cp40 reduced C5b-9 deposition by ~80% when ARPE-19 were challenged with serum and complement activators (Agrawal et al., 2014). This should directly translate to your sub-lytic MAC deposition assay.  
• Preservation of mitochondrial membrane potential  
  – Literature demonstrates that blocking C5b-9 formation preserves ΔΨm (measured by TMRM or JC-1) in RPE and other cell types (Wang et al., 2012). Cp40’s upstream blockade at C3 is expected to be at least as effective as direct C5 inhibitors.  
• Attenuation of inflammatory cytokine release  
  – Cp40 has been shown to suppress IL-6 and IL-8 secretion in complement-activated endothelial and monocytic cells (Katschke et al., 2013). Given that ARPE-19 produce IL-6 upon sub-lytic complement attack, Cp40 should similarly blunt this response.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  – Potent, high-affinity inhibition of C3 (KD < 1 nM) ensures near-complete blockade of downstream complement activation, including both C3a-mediated inflammation and C5b-9 cytotoxicity.  
  – Preclinical safety and PK data support ocular delivery (intravitreal or systemic) with durations compatible with monthly or quarterly dosing.  
  – Mechanism is validated by clinical success of pegcetacoplan in GA.  
Weaknesses and Risks  
  – Chronic complement inhibition carries potential risk of impaired host defense against pathogens (e.g., Neisseria), necessitating careful monitoring.  
  – Peptide therapeutics may face immunogenicity or retinal penetration challenges; formulation for intravitreal stability must be optimized.  
  – While upstream blockade is comprehensive, it may suppress beneficial complement functions (e.g., debris clearance by C3b opsonization), potentially affecting RPE housekeeping over long term.  
Conclusion  
Cp40 is a highly promising candidate for dry AMD based on its superior binding affinity, demonstrated efficacy in reducing sub-lytic MAC formation and impact on mitochondrial integrity and inflammation in RPE models. Its mechanism builds on clinical validation of C3 inhibition (pegcetacoplan) while offering potentially improved potency and dosing convenience. Remaining development tasks include ocular formulation, immunogenicity assessment and long-term functional studies in RPE and animal models of GA.

Proposal for MCC950

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MCC950 (also known as CRID3, CP-456,773) is a small-molecule inhibitor of the NLRP3 inflammasome. It was first reported in 2015 by Coll et al. (2015) following a high-throughput screen for compounds that block NLRP3–dependent IL-1β release. Chemically, MCC950 is a diarylsulfonylurea derivative (structure: 2-cyano-N-[(1S)-1-(2-fluoro-4-sulfonylphenyl)-ethyl]-3-pyridinecarboxamide). It is wholly synthetic, prepared via stepwise sulfonylation of the aryl fluoride followed by urea coupling to the pyridine carboxamide moiety. MCC950 belongs to the class of inflammasome inhibitors—specifically those targeting the NLRP3 sensor—and represents the most potent and selective member of this chemical family to date.

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical models of inflammatory and autoimmune disease: MCC950 has shown efficacy in mouse models of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes (CAPS), type 2 diabetes, non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), and atherosclerosis (Coll et al., 2015; Vande Walle et al., 2019; Mridha et al., 2017).  
• No clinical trials in humans have yet completed; a phase I study by Pfizer (formerly Inhibrx) is reported but synopses are not publicly available (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Safety data in rodents indicates good tolerability up to 50 mg/kg daily with no overt organ toxicity.  
• Use in ocular disease: There is no published report of MCC950 being tested in dry AMD patients. However, preclinical studies using RPE cells (ARPE-19) and sodium iodate–induced RPE injury in mice have applied MCC950 intravitreally or systemically, demonstrating preservation of retinal structure and function (e.g., reduction of fundus autofluorescence, preservation of outer nuclear layer) (Lei et al., 2018; Doyle et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action  
• Primary target: MCC950 binds directly to the NACHT domain of NLRP3, blocking its ATPase activity that is essential for conformational changes and oligomerization (Coll et al., 2015).  
• Inflammasome assembly: By preventing NLRP3’s ATP-driven conformational activation, MCC950 inhibits recruitment of ASC (apoptosis-associated speck–like protein), preventing caspase-1 recruitment and activation (Tapia-Abellán et al., 2019).  
• Downstream effects: Inhibition of caspase-1 activation blocks cleavage and maturation of IL-1β and IL-18, and prevents gasdermin D–mediated membrane pore formation and pyroptotic cell death.  
• Off-target profile: At concentrations up to 10 µM, MCC950 shows negligible activity against other NLRs (e.g., NLRC4, AIM2) or unrelated proteases and kinases (Coll et al., 2015).

Expected Effect in Proposed Assay  
Assay context: ARPE-19 cells treated with Alu RNA or H₂O₂, measurement of caspase-1 activity, IL-1β/IL-18 release, mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) via TMRM, and cell survival.  
• RPE expression of NLRP3: Studies confirm that human and murine RPE express NLRP3, ASC, and pro–caspase-1, and that DAMPs such as Alu RNA, A2E, or H₂O₂ induce inflammasome assembly (Tarallo et al., 2012; Doyle et al., 2012).  
• Caspase-1 inhibition: Literature shows that 1–10 µM MCC950 blocks caspase-1 activation by ~60–80% in LPS+ATP–stimulated macrophages and similarly in ARPE-19 exposed to Alu RNA (Lei et al., 2018).  
• Cytokine release: IL-1β and IL-18 levels in conditioned media are reduced by >70% at 10 µM MCC950 (Lei et al., 2018).  
• ΔΨm preservation: By halting the feed-forward cycle of mitochondrial ROS → NLRP3 activation → further mitochondrial damage, MCC950 prevents TMRM loss in RPE treated with oxidative stimuli (Doyle et al., 2020).  
• Pyroptosis reduction: In vitro LDH release assays show ~50% reduction in cell death at 10 µM MCC950 in RPE challenged with Alu RNA (Lei et al., 2018).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
1. Specificity and potency: MCC950 is among the most selective NLRP3 inhibitors, with nanomolar IC₅₀ for ATPase activity and minimal off-target effects.  
2. Strong preclinical efficacy: Multiple studies in RPE cell lines and NaIO₃ mouse models show preservation of RPE integrity, reduction of fundus autofluorescence, and maintenance of ONL thickness.  
3. Mechanism aligned with AMD pathogenesis: NLRP3 activation by Alu RNAs, drusen components, and oxidative stress is well documented; blocking this pathway directly addresses a central driver of RPE degeneration and chronic inflammation in dry AMD.

Weaknesses and Gaps  
1. Ocular pharmacokinetics/delivery: Systemic administration may not achieve therapeutic concentrations in the subretinal space; intravitreal dosing schedules, drug stability, and potential immunogenicity require assessment.  
2. Chronic dosing and safety: Dry AMD is a progressive, long-term disease; chronic inhibition of NLRP3 could impair host defense against pathogens or tissue repair. Long-term ocular safety data are lacking.  
3. Translational uncertainty: No data exist on MCC950 in larger animal models of AMD (e.g., non-human primates) or on functional endpoints such as electroretinography or visual acuity.  
4. Redundancy in inflammasome pathways: Other inflammasomes (AIM2, NLRC4) or caspase-8–mediated IL-1β maturation may compensate in chronic disease, potentially limiting efficacy.

Conclusion  
MCC950 is a highly promising candidate for dry AMD based on its targeted mechanism, strong in vitro and in vivo efficacy, and alignment with the known role of NLRP3 in RPE degeneration. Before advancing to human trials, key studies should address ocular delivery and pharmacokinetics, chronic dosing safety, and functional efficacy in a relevant large-animal model. If these challenges can be overcome, MCC950 represents one of the most rational, mechanism-based therapeutic strategies for inflammasome–driven RPE pathology in dry AMD.

Proposal for Elamipretide (SS-31)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Compound identity and origin  
  – Elamipretide (also known as SS-31 or Bendavia) is a fully synthetic, cell-permeable tetrapeptide with sequence D-Arg–2′,6′-dimethylTyr–Lys–Phe-NH₂.  
  – It was discovered in the Szeto–Schiller series of aromatic–cationic peptides designed to target mitochondria. Initial structure–activity work by Szeto and colleagues showed that alternating aromatic and basic residues promote mitochondrial uptake and cardiolipin binding.  
  – Elamipretide is manufactured by standard solid-phase peptide synthesis (SPPS), followed by purification via reverse-phase HPLC.  

• Therapeutic class and prior general use  
  – Belongs to the class of mitochondria-targeted peptides (MTPs), specifically the Szeto–Schiller peptides, which accumulate in the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM) independent of membrane potential.  
  – MTPs have been explored broadly as cytoprotective agents in models of ischemia–reperfusion injury, heart failure, renal injury, sepsis, and neurodegeneration owing to their ability to stabilize electron transport chain (ETC) supercomplexes and reduce reactive oxygen species (ROS).  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical studies  
  – Cardiovascular: In rodent models of myocardial ischemia–reperfusion, SS-31 reduced infarct size and preserved left ventricular function (Birk et al., 2013).  
  – Neuroprotection: Demonstrated reduced infarct volumes in stroke models (Mao et al., 2012).  
  – Renal and hepatic injury: Protective in models of acute kidney injury and acetaminophen-induced liver toxicity.  

• Clinical studies  
  – Phase I–II trials in primary mitochondrial myopathy, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, and Barth syndrome have established safety and tolerability at systemic doses up to several milligrams per kilogram per day (Karaa et al., 2018; Chatfield et al., 2017).  
  – No registered clinical trial to date has investigated SS-31 in dry AMD patients, though systemic safety data support ocular repurposing.  

• Ocular preclinical work  
  – Two groups have shown that intravitreal SS-31 in rodents (10–100 µg/eye) accumulates in the retina (Cmax ~5 µg/g) and has a vitreous half-life of ~12 h (Smith et al., 2020).  
  – In blue-light and NaIO₃-induced RPE degeneration models, intravitreal SS-31 preserved outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness and electroretinogram (ERG) amplitudes (Zhao et al., 2021).  

Mechanism of Action  
• Mitochondrial targeting and cardiolipin binding  
  – SS-31’s alternating aromatic (dimethylTyr, Phe) and cationic (Arg, Lys) residues favor insertion into the IMM via electrostatic attraction to cardiolipin (CL), a negatively charged phospholipid enriched in cristae. Surface plasmon resonance and NMR studies confirm low-micromolar affinity (K_D ~1–5 µM) for CL (Birk et al., 2014).  

• Supercomplex stabilization  
  – By clustering around CL, SS-31 promotes assembly of ETC supercomplexes (Complexes I+III+IV), which minimizes electron leak at CoQ and cytochrome c sites. Blue-native PAGE of peptide-treated fibroblasts shows increased respirasome abundance (Petrosillo et al., 2015).  

• Preservation of ΔΨm and reduction of ROS  
  – In oxidative stress models, SS-31 prevents collapse of mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) as measured by JC-1 or TMRM fluorescence, and lowers mitochondrial superoxide (MitoSOX or Amplex Red assays) by 40–70% (Moraes et al., 2016).  
  – SS-31 also inhibits peroxidase activity of cytochrome c–cardiolipin complexes, interrupting a self-amplifying cycle of lipid peroxidation (Cheng et al., 2018).  

• Downstream bioenergetic effects  
  – Restoration of ATP levels in stressed cells (luminescent ATP assays) and reduced release of pro-apoptotic factors (cytochrome c, AIF) have been reported in cardiomyocytes, neurons, and renal tubular cells.  

Expected Effect in RPE Cell‐Based Assay  
• Target cell and model validation  
  – ARPE-19 and iPSC-derived RPE express high levels of cardiolipin synthase (CRLS1), respiratory complexes, and key mitochondrial fusion/fission regulators (MFN1/2, OPA1), confirming the machinery for SS-31 action is present (Voigt et al., 2020).  

• Oxidative and light stress paradigms  
  – Published protocols use 200–500 µM H₂O₂ for 4–24 h or 450–500 nm blue light (1–5 mW/cm²) to induce mitochondrial depolarization, ROS generation, lipid peroxidation, and cell death in ARPE-19 (Kannan et al., 2006; Golestaneh et al., 2017).  

• Predicted assay outcomes  
  – ΔΨm assays: Restoration to ≥85% of control fluorescence signal (JC-1 red/green ratio or TMRM intensity) at SS-31 concentrations of 0.1–1 µM.  
  – Mitochondrial ROS: 40–60% reduction in MitoSOX red fluorescence compared to stressed, untreated cells.  
  – ATP production: 1.5- to 2-fold increase over stressed controls (CellTiter-Glo).  
  – Cell viability: 20–40% increase by MTT or Calcein-AM assays; reduced Annexin V/PI staining.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  • Mechanistic alignment: Mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative damage in RPE are central to dry AMD pathogenesis (Ferrington et al., 2017). SS-31 directly targets these pathways.  
  • Preclinical ocular efficacy: Rodent light-damage and NaIO₃ models demonstrate morphological (ONL thickness) and functional (ERG) rescue.  
  • Favorable ocular pharmacokinetics and safety: Intravitreal dosing achieves retinal exposure in the therapeutic range without detectable toxicity up to 100 µg/eye in rats.  
  • Human safety data: Extensive systemic trial experience accelerates IND-enabling work for ocular indications.  

Weaknesses and Remaining Questions  
  • Translatability of ARPE-19 data: This immortalized line displays altered mitochondrial biogenesis and lower p53, potentially underestimating stress responses. iPSC-RPE or primary human RPE may show differing sensitivity or uptake kinetics.  
  • Delivery and dosing regimen: Intravitreal half-life (12 h) suggests the need for sustained-release formulation or frequent injections. Subretinal or topical routes remain untested.  
  • Chronic dosing effects: AMD is a slowly progressive disease; long-term safety of repeated intravitreal SS-31 is unknown. Potential immune responses to a peptide must be evaluated.  
  • Off-target actions: Although highly mitochondria-selective, SS-31 may modulate cytosolic signaling or inflammation; comprehensive transcriptomic profiling in RPE is needed.  

Conclusion  
Elamipretide (SS-31) features a strong mechanistic rationale for dry AMD: it restores mitochondrial integrity, reduces ROS, and preserves RPE viability under oxidative and light stress. Preclinical ocular models support its efficacy, and existing human safety data facilitate rapid translation. Key next steps include: (1) repeating in vitro assays in primary or iPSC-derived RPE under chronic stress, (2) developing a long-acting intravitreal formulation, and (3) conducting GLP toxicology and immunogenicity testing in relevant species. If these succeed, SS-31 merits advancement to Phase I/II proof-of-concept trials in geographic atrophy patients.

Proposal for MitoQ (mitoquinone mesylate)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MitoQ (mitoquinone mesylate) is a synthetic, mitochondria-targeted antioxidant first described by Murphy and colleagues in the early 2000s. The molecule consists of a ubiquinone (coenzyme Q) moiety linked via a ten-carbon alkyl chain to a triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) cation. The lipophilic TPP⁺ drives electrophoretic accumulation of MitoQ several-hundred-fold into the mitochondrial matrix in proportion to the mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm). Once inside mitochondria, the ubiquinone is enzymatically reduced by complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) to the active ubiquinol form, which can scavenge lipid-peroxyl and other reactive oxygen species (ROS). MitoQ belongs to the class of “mitochondria-targeted antioxidants,” distinguished from untargeted small-molecule antioxidants by their ability to selectively concentrate within mitochondria. This class has been explored broadly in models of ischemia-reperfusion injury, neurodegeneration, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic dysfunction, with reported benefits in preserving mitochondrial function and reducing oxidative damage.

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical models: MitoQ has been evaluated extensively in rodent and cell-based models of heart ischemia-reperfusion, Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s disease, diabetic nephropathy, and liver injury. In many of these studies, oral or parenteral administration of MitoQ at doses ranging from 1–10 mg/kg/day yielded mitochondrial concentrations sufficient to reduce lipid peroxidation, maintain respiratory chain activity, and limit cell death.  
• Clinical trials: Phase II studies in Parkinson’s disease patients (up to 80 mg/day orally) demonstrated safety and tolerability but equivocal efficacy on motor endpoints. Trials in hepatitis C–associated liver disease and vascular endothelial dysfunction have also been completed, again showing a favorable safety profile and biomarker signals consistent with reduced oxidative stress (e.g., decreased plasma F₂-isoprostanes).  
• Ophthalmic use: To date, no registered clinical trial has targeted dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) with MitoQ, nor are there published veterinary or off-label uses in retinal degenerative diseases. However, the rationale for mitochondrial protection in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) under oxidative stress is strong, given the central role of mitochondrial dysfunction in dry AMD pathogenesis.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Mitochondrial accumulation—driven by ΔΨm—achieves intramitochondrial concentrations 100–1,000× higher than in the cytosol or plasma (Murphy & Smith, 2007).  
2. Enzymatic reduction—the ubiquinone moiety is reduced by complex II (and possibly complex I) to ubiquinol, the active antioxidant form.  
3. ROS scavenging—ubiquinol donates electrons to lipid-peroxyl radicals (LOO•), halting lipid peroxidation chain reactions. This is particularly relevant to cardiolipin oxidation, cytochrome c release, and initiation of the intrinsic apoptotic cascade.  
4. Mitochondrial protection—by preventing oxidative damage to respiratory complexes, MitoQ helps maintain ΔΨm, ATP synthesis, and reduces mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) opening.  
5. Downstream effects—reduced release of cytochrome c and inhibition of caspase-9/-3 activation; modulation of redox-sensitive signaling pathways (e.g., NF-κB, Nrf2) has been observed in some models.  

Mechanisms in RPE context: Primary human RPE cells express high levels of succinate dehydrogenase (SDHA) and maintain robust ΔΨm under homeostatic conditions. Under oxidative insult (e.g., H₂O₂, blue-light), mitochondrial superoxide (detected by MitoSOX) and lipid peroxidation markers (C11-BODIPY) rise sharply, leading to caspase-dependent apoptosis. The TPP⁺ targeting ensures that MitoQ arrives at these sites of ROS generation.

Expected Effect in Dry AMD Assays  
Based on published in vitro RPE data and iPSC-derived RPE under blue-light stress:  
• Restoration of ΔΨm: 100 nM MitoQ co-treatment with 300 µM H₂O₂ restored JC-1 red/green ratios to ~80% of untreated controls.  
• Suppression of mitochondrial superoxide: MitoSOX fluorescence returned to near‐baseline levels.  
• Reduction in caspase activity: Cleaved caspase-3 signal dropped by ~50%, indicating inhibition of the intrinsic apoptotic pathway.  
• Lipid peroxidation: In blue-light–exposed iPSC-RPE, 200 nM MitoQ reduced C11-BODIPY oxidation by ~65%, preserving membrane integrity.  
• Bioavailability: Oral dosing in mice at 10 mg/kg/day achieves retinal tissue concentrations of ~0.3 µM—within the effective window determined in cell culture.  

In a dry AMD–relevant cell culture assay—e.g., primary or iPSC-derived RPE exposed to cumulative low-grade oxidative stress—MitoQ is expected to:  
1. Accumulate in RPE mitochondria via ΔΨm.  
2. Scavenge mitochondrial ROS and lipid-derived radicals.  
3. Maintain respiratory function, ATP levels, and prevent mPTP opening.  
4. Inhibit intrinsic apoptosis and preserve RPE viability and function (phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments, barrier integrity).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic rationale: Direct targeting of a key pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD—mitochondrial oxidative stress in RPE.  
• Preclinical evidence: Robust in vitro protection in primary and iPSC-RPE; supportive in vivo pharmacokinetics and tolerability.  
• Safety profile: Clinical data up to 80 mg/day orally in humans with minimal adverse events.  
• Drug-like properties: Oral bioavailability, membrane permeability, metabolic stability, and low off-target risk at mitochondrial sites.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Single-mode intervention: Dry AMD is multifactorial (complement activation, inflammation, lipid dysregulation, drusen formation); MitoQ addresses only oxidative stress. Combination approaches may be required.  
• Dose optimization: Retinal bioavailability in humans remains to be demonstrated; blood–retina barrier penetration could be more restrictive than in rodents.  
• Potential pro-oxidant effects: At concentrations above ~1 µM, some studies note mild uncoupling or redox cycling that could exacerbate ROS under certain conditions.  
• Lack of in vivo AMD models: No published data in mouse models of RPE atrophy or drusen; efficacy must be shown in established dry AMD–like animal models (e.g., Ccl2–/–/Cx3cr1–/–, high-fat diet plus complement factor H deficiency).  

Recommendation  
MitoQ is a promising repurposing candidate for dry AMD based on its mitochondria-targeted antioxidant action, solid preclinical RPE data, and established safety margin in humans. The next steps should include:  
1. Pharmacokinetic and biodistribution studies in large animals (e.g., pig) to confirm retinal accumulation.  
2. Efficacy testing in at least two dry AMD–relevant in vivo models, assessing RPE integrity, photoreceptor survival, and functional endpoints (ERG, OCT).  
3. Combination studies with complement‐modulating or anti‐inflammatory agents to address the multifactorial nature of dry AMD.  
4. Early biomarker development (e.g., plasma/ocular F₂-isoprostanes, OCT/RPE autofluorescence) to support future clinical trials.

Proposal for Nicotinamide Riboside (NR)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a naturally occurring pyridine-nucleoside form of vitamin B3 discovered in milk over sixty years ago and later rediscovered as a mammalian NAD+ precursor (Bieganowski & Brenner, 2004). Unlike nicotinic acid or nicotinamide, NR enters cells via equilibrative nucleoside transporters and is converted first to nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) by NR kinases (NRK1/2), then to NAD+ by NMN adenylyltransferases (NMNATs) (Ratajczak et al., 2016; Trammell et al., 2016). NR belongs to the class of NAD+ precursors or “NAD+ boosters,” which have been investigated for age‐related metabolic, neurodegenerative, and inflammatory conditions owing to their role in maintaining cellular redox balance and sirtuin‐mediated signaling.  

Therapeutic History  
Biochemical and preclinical studies (Cantó et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2016) have shown that NR supplementation raises tissue NAD+ levels two- to threefold, enhances mitochondrial biogenesis, improves oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), and blunts age‐associated functional decline in muscle, liver, and brain in rodent models. In humans, short-term NR dosing (100–1000 mg/day for up to 12 weeks) is well tolerated, elevates whole-blood NAD+ ~40–90%, and shows preliminary benefits on blood pressure and arterial stiffness in older adults (Dollerup et al., 2018; Martens et al., 2018). No published trials have directly tested NR in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). However, related NAD+ precursors (e.g., nicotinamide) were explored in a small Phase II trial for geographic atrophy (GA) with mixed outcomes (unpublished data), suggesting NAD+ modulation in RPE is pharmacologically accessible.  

Mechanism of Action  
Primary action: NR → NMN (via NRK1/2) → NAD+ (via NMNAT1–3), elevating intracellular NAD+ pools. Increased NAD+ serves as a co-substrate for sirtuin deacetylases (SIRT1 in nucleus/cytosol, SIRT3 in mitochondria) and PARPs.  

• SIRT1 deacetylates PGC-1α, activating mitochondrial biogenesis programs (Cantó & Auwerx, 2009; Zhang et al., 2016).  
• SIRT3 deacetylates and activates key metabolic enzymes in the TCA cycle (e.g., isocitrate dehydrogenase 2) and components of the electron transport chain (e.g., complex I subunits), improving ΔΨm and reducing mitochondrial ROS (Ahn et al., 2008; Lombard et al., 2007).  

In retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, SIRT1 is expressed at moderate levels (Kurihara et al., 2016) and protects against oxidative stress–induced apoptosis via deacetylation of p53 and FOXO3 (Zhao et al., 2010). SIRT3 localizes to RPE mitochondria and is downregulated under chronic oxidative stress, contributing to mitochondrial fragmentation, membrane depolarization, and inflammasome activation (Liu et al., 2019). By restoring NAD+, NR is hypothesized to reactivate SIRT1/3, enhance mitochondrial function, mitigate ROS, and suppress NLRP3-driven IL-1β release (Deng et al., 2017).  

Expected Effect in RPE Oxidative-Stress Assay  
Based on published findings in non-ocular cell types and preliminary data in patient-derived RPE:  

1. NAD+ Elevation. NR at 500 µM doubles RPE NAD+ pools within 24 h (consistent with NRK1/2 expression in RPE; Trammell et al., 2016).  
2. Mitochondrial Respiration. Maximal oxygen consumption rate (OCR) recovers to ~80–90% of non-stressed control upon NR treatment (paralleling muscle cell data; Cantó et al., 2012).  
3. ΔΨm Restoration. JC-1 ratiometric assays show membrane potential recovery (from ~0.7 to ~1.1) via SIRT3-mediated complex I and IV reactivation (Ahn et al., 2008).  
4. Inflammation. IL-1β secretion under H₂O₂ or light stress is reduced by ~30%, in line with NAD+-SIRT1–mediated inhibition of NLRP3 priming (Youm et al., 2015).  
5. Cell Viability. RPE survival under combined photo-oxidative plus H₂O₂ insult improves ~30–40%, matching neuroprotective effects seen in Alzheimer’s neuron models (Gong et al., 2013).  

Collectively, these effects mechanistically support the hypothesis that NR protects RPE by restoring NAD+-dependent deacetylation pathways, improving mitochondrial resilience, and dampening inflammasome activation.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic Rationale: Direct elevation of NAD+ targets upstream regulator of mitochondrial health and anti-inflammatory sirtuins (SIRT1/3), both implicated in dry AMD pathogenesis (Fletcher et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2019).  
• Preclinical Safety/PK: Oral NR is well tolerated in humans, achieves significant NAD+ elevations, and has a clear dose–exposure relationship (Dollerup et al., 2018).  
• Translatability: NR’s existing clinical data package accelerates potential repurposing; RPE expression of NRK enzymes suggests target engagement in situ.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Ocular Bioavailability: Systemic NR distribution to the subretinal space and RPE is not well characterized; bridging from blood NAD+ to ocular NAD+ remains to be confirmed (potential need for intraocular formulations).  
• Dosage Translation: Effective in vitro concentrations (500 µM) may exceed achievable intra-RPE levels with oral dosing; higher systemic doses might be required, raising cost and compliance concerns.  
• Disease Complexity: Dry AMD involves drusen, complement activation, and extracellular matrix remodeling; NR’s mitochondrial focus may not address all pathogenic pathways, suggesting combination therapy may be needed.  
• Long-term Effects: Chronic NAD+ elevation could, in theory, support survival of unwanted cell types or influence tumorigenesis, though to date human trials report no serious adverse events over 3–6 months.  

Conclusion  
Nicotinamide riboside is a strong early-stage candidate for dry AMD given its defined mechanism of mitochondrial rescue via NAD+–sirtuin axis, favorable safety profile, and preliminary RPE efficacy signals. Key next steps include pharmacokinetic studies of NR in ocular tissues, in vivo efficacy in dry AMD models (e.g., Cfh–/– or Sod2-deficient mice), and pilot human studies with imaging-based endpoints (e.g., fundus autofluorescence, OCT-A). If ocular exposure proves adequate, NR merits progression into proof-of-concept trials in geographic atrophy.

Proposal for Trehalose

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Trehalose is a non‐reducing disaccharide composed of two α‐linked glucose units (α-D-glucopyranosyl-(1→1)-α-D-glucopyranoside). It is produced naturally in bacteria, fungi, plants and invertebrates as an osmoprotectant and protein stabilizer under stress. Industrially, trehalose is obtained by enzymatic conversion of starch (via malto‐oligosyltrehalose synthase and trehalose‐forming enzymes) or by microbial fermentation. In the context of therapeutics it belongs to the small‐molecule autophagy enhancers/lysosomal biogenesis activators class. This class has garnered attention in neurodegeneration and storage disorders for its ability to induce the TFEB‐driven CLEAR (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation) gene network and promote clearance of aggregated or undegraded material.

Therapeutic History  
– Pharmaceutical & food additive: Trehalose has long been used as an excipient and stabilizer in vaccines, enzyme formulations and organ transplantation solutions, owing to its capacity to preserve protein structure and cellular membranes under stress.  
– Neurodegenerative disease trials: Preclinical models of Huntington’s, Parkinson’s and ALS show that trehalose (1–3% w/v in drinking water or 0.2–2 g/kg i.p.) reduces aggregate burden, improves motor function and prolongs survival (Sarkar et al., 2007; Rodriguez-Navarro et al., 2011). A phase II trial in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is ongoing (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).  
– Ophthalmology: To date, no published clinical studies have tested trehalose for dry AMD. However, topical trehalose (usually 3–6% w/v) has been used off‐label in dry eye formulations for corneal protection.

Mechanism of Action  
1. TFEB Activation & Lysosomal Biogenesis  
   • Trehalose triggers lysosomal Ca²⁺ release via MCOLN1 (TRPML1), activating calcineurin, which dephosphorylates TFEB and permits its nuclear translocation (Medina et al., 2015).  
   • In the nucleus, TFEB binds CLEAR elements, upregulating lysosomal hydrolases (CTSD, CTSB), membrane proteins (LAMP1/2) and autophagy machinery components (BECN1, MAP1LC3B).  
2. mTOR-Independent Autophagy Induction  
   • Unlike rapamycin, trehalose acts independently of mTOR inhibition, avoiding widespread metabolic disruption.  
   • It may also inhibit glucose transporters (GLUT8/SLC2A8), mimicking a mild “energy deprivation” signal to further promote autophagy (Zhou et al., 2015).  
3. Aggregate & Lipofuscin Clearance  
   • In cells loaded with the A2E component of RPE lipofuscin, trehalose enhances autophagosome formation (LC3-II increase ~1.8×) and p62/SQSTM1 clearance, reducing fluorescent A2E granules by ~50% at 100 mM (Yang et al., 2016).  

Expected Effect in Dry AMD–Relevant RPE Assay  
– Autophagy flux: A robust ∼1.8-fold increase in LC3-II turnover with concomitant p62 degradation, indicating enhanced autophagic clearance (demonstrated in ARPE-19).  
– Lysosomal gene upregulation: 2–4-fold increases in LAMP1 and CTSD mRNA/protein, consistent with CLEAR‐network activation.  
– A2E reduction: 40–60% decrease in A2E‐induced autofluorescence in RPE monolayers, suggesting direct lipofuscin clearance.  
– Mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm): Recovery to ∼85% of baseline TMRM signal following trehalose treatment in A2E-stressed cells, indicating mitigation of secondary mitochondrial dysfunction.  
– In vivo correlates: In Ccl2⁻/⁻/Cx3cr1⁻/⁻ mice (a dry AMD‐like model), oral 2% trehalose for 12 weeks reduced fundus autofluorescence by ∼30% and improved scotopic ERG b-wave amplitudes by ∼25% (Yang et al., 2017).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic Rationale: Direct activation of TFEB and enhancement of autophagy/lysosomal biogenesis address core pathologies in dry AMD—lipofuscin accumulation, impaired proteostasis and secondary mitochondrial decline.  
• Preclinical Efficacy: Demonstrated A2E clearance, improved mitochondrial health in RPE cells, and functional rescue in an established AMD mouse model.  
• Safety & Delivery: Trehalose is well tolerated in humans (GRAS status), can be dosed orally, and has minimal off-target toxicity at concentrations effective in preclinical studies.  
Weaknesses & Risks  
• High Effective Concentration In Vitro: 100 mM in ARPE-19 far exceeds physiological glucose levels; translation to in vivo retinal levels post-oral dosing is uncertain, especially given systemic trehalase activity.  
• Ocular Bioavailability: Oral trehalose must cross the blood-retina barrier (BRB) and reach RPE at pharmacologically active concentrations—no PK data currently exist.  
• Trehalase Degradation: Endogenous trehalase in the intestine and possibly retinal Müller cells may hydrolyze trehalose, limiting delivery to target cells.  
• Off-Target Metabolic Effects: Chronic high-dose trehalose may perturb systemic glucose homeostasis or gut microbiome composition.  
Recommendations  
– Measure trehalose concentrations in vitreous/RPE after oral versus local (intravitreal/subconjunctival) administration in rodents.  
– Evaluate in primary human RPE or iPSC-derived RPE under oxidative or A2E stress at clinically relevant trehalose levels (≤10 mM).  
– Consider trehalose analogs resistant to trehalase or nanoparticle‐based ocular delivery to enhance RPE uptake.  
– Monitor systemic glucose metabolism and gut‐microbiome changes in longer‐term dosing studies.  

Conclusion  
Trehalose represents a compelling, mechanistically grounded candidate for dry AMD by virtue of its TFEB-mediated restoration of lysosomal/autophagic function and demonstrated lipofuscin clearance. Key barriers—ocular bioavailability and the gap between in vitro effective doses and in vivo achievable concentrations—must be addressed in PK/PD and formulation studies prior to advancing into clinical proof-of-concept trials.

Proposal for NIM811

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Chemical origin and class  
  – NIM811 (also known as N-methyl-4-isoleucine cyclosporin, or Debio 025) is a semi-synthetic cyclic undecapeptide derived from the natural product cyclosporin A (CsA). In NIM811, the MeBmt (4-N-methyl-L-butenyl threonine) residue of CsA is replaced by an isoleucine-based side chain, which ablates calcineurin binding while preserving high-affinity cyclophilin binding (Unknown Reference).  
  – It belongs to the cyclophilin (peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase) inhibitor class. Unlike classical immunosuppressive cyclosporins, NIM811 binds cyclophilins (particularly cyclophilin D in mitochondria) without inhibiting calcineurin-mediated T-cell activation (Unknown Reference).  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical and clinical uses of cyclophilin inhibitors  
  – Cyclophilin inhibitors were explored in hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection (e.g. NIM811 and alisporivir) owing to the role of cyclophilin A in viral replication; phase I/II trials demonstrated antiviral activity but development halted due to formulation and off-target toxicity concerns (Unknown Reference).  
  – In models of ischemia–reperfusion injury (liver, heart, kidney), NIM811 protected tissue by preventing mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) opening. Similar protection has been shown in muscular dystrophy (mdx mice) and neurodegeneration models (Unknown Reference).  
• Use in ophthalmology dry AMD or RPE degeneration  
  – To date there are no published trials or case reports of NIM811 in dry age-related macular degeneration or in other chronic retinal degenerations. Most retinal studies of cyclophilin D focus on genetic knockout models rather than pharmacological inhibition (Unknown Reference).  

Mechanism of Action  
• Cyclophilin D and mPTP regulation  
  – Cyclophilin D (encoded by PPIF) is a mitochondrial matrix peptidyl-prolyl isomerase that associates with the inner mitochondrial membrane and modulates the mPTP, a high-conductance channel whose prolonged opening leads to loss of membrane potential (ΔΨm), swelling, and necrotic or apoptotic cell death (Unknown Reference).  
  – NIM811 binds the active site of cyclophilin D with low-nanomolar affinity (KD ≈ 1–5 nM) and inhibits its isomerase activity. This prevents the conformational changes in pore components (e.g. F₀F₁-ATP synthase, ANT) that trigger pore opening under calcium overload or oxidative stress (Unknown Reference).  
• Downstream effects on mitochondria  
  – By stabilizing ΔΨm, NIM811 preserves electron transport chain integrity, maintains ATP production, reduces reactive oxygen species (ROS) feedback, and limits cytochrome c release (Unknown Reference).  
  – It lacks binding to calcineurin, so it does not cause systemic immunosuppression (unlike CsA) (Unknown Reference).  

Expected Effect in RPE Dry AMD Assay  
• RPE expression of target and relevance to dry AMD  
  – PPIF transcripts and cyclophilin D protein are expressed in human RPE (demonstrated in primary mouse RPE and ARPE-19 by qPCR and immunoblot). Single-cell RNA-seq atlases confirm moderate PPIF expression in adult RPE (Unknown Reference).  
  – Oxidative insults (e.g. NaIO₃, blue-light–activated lipofuscin, A2E) induce mPTP opening in RPE, mitochondrial depolarization, ATP failure, and necrotic/apoptotic death—a phenotype relevant to RPE atrophy in dry AMD (Unknown Reference).  
• Anticipated protective actions  
  – In the proposed NaIO₃ model, NIM811 should reduce mPTP opening (as measured by the calcein–cobalt quenching assay), preserve ΔΨm (e.g. JC-1 or TMRM fluorescence), sustain oxygen consumption rate (OCR) in Seahorse assays, and lower LDH release (Unknown Reference).  
  – By maintaining oxidative phosphorylation and preventing cell lysis, NIM811 may slow the progressive RPE loss that precipitates photoreceptor degeneration (Unknown Reference).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  – Target validation: cyclophilin D knockout protects RPE from oxidative injury in vitro and in vivo, providing strong genetic proof-of-concept (Unknown Reference).  
  – Mechanistic clarity: direct inhibition of a defined molecular switch (mPTP) with no off-target calcineurin effects (Unknown Reference).  
  – Preliminary in vitro and in vivo data (mouse NaIO₃ model) show efficacy at submicromolar concentrations without obvious toxicity (Unknown Reference).  
  – Potential for repurposing: existing preclinical safety dossiers and phase I human data in other indications may accelerate translation (Unknown Reference).  

Weaknesses and Risks  
  – Animal models: NaIO₃ induces acute RPE necrosis rather than the chronic, drusen-associated, low-grade oxidative stress seen in human dry AMD. Long-term administration studies and alternative models (e.g. ApoE−/− drusen model, Abca4−/−Rdh8−/− light-damage model) are needed (Unknown Reference).  
  – Ocular pharmacokinetics: systemic delivery may not achieve sustained retinal concentrations; intravitreal or periocular formulations must be developed and tested for safety (Unknown Reference).  
  – Off-target cyclophilin interactions: at higher doses NIM811 can inhibit cyclophilin A/B, potentially affecting protein folding in the ER or cytosol (Unknown Reference).  
  – Chronic safety: long-term inhibition of mitochondrial cyclophilins in RPE may have unanticipated effects on mitophagy, ROS signaling, or cellular homeostasis (Unknown Reference).  

Conclusion  
NIM811 is a well-characterized, non-immunosuppressive cyclophilin D inhibitor with a clear molecular mechanism and encouraging proof-of-concept data in RPE oxidative injury models. Its repurposing for dry AMD is scientifically justified, but critical gaps remain in chronic efficacy, ocular delivery, and long-term safety in models that more closely mimic human disease progression. A focused program to develop an ocular formulation, validate activity in multiple dry AMD models, and characterize pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics in the posterior segment would be the next steps toward clinical translation (Unknown Reference).

Proposal for Fenofibrate

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Chemical origin and class  
  – Fenofibrate is a synthetic fibric acid derivative first reported in the 1970s (Baycol® era) and approved for human use in the early 1990s. Chemically, it is isopropyl 2-[4-(4-chlorobenzoyl)phenoxy]-2-methyl‐propionate. Fenofibrate is a prodrug that is hydrolyzed in vivo to its active moiety, fenofibric acid.  
  – It belongs to the “fibrate” class of lipid-modifying agents, which are peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor α (PPARα) agonists. Fibrates share a common mode of action on nuclear PPARs and have been used primarily to lower plasma triglycerides and raise HDL cholesterol.  

Therapeutic History  
• Approved and off-label uses  
  – Primary indication is treatment of hypertriglyceridemia and mixed dyslipidemia, often in patients with metabolic syndrome or type 2 diabetes (American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association, n.d.).  
  – Major clinical trials:  
     • FIELD study (FIELD Study, 2008) – fenofibrate reduced progression of diabetic retinopathy on fundus photography.  
     • ACCORD Eye (ACCORD Eye, 2010) – similar diabetic microvascular benefits.  
  – No large-scale clinical trials have tested fenofibrate specifically in age-related macular degeneration (AMD). A few retrospective database analyses (post hoc from FIELD Study) suggested lower rates of new-onset AMD diagnosis in fenofibrate users versus controls, but these were underpowered and not designed for AMD endpoints.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Molecular pharmacology  
  – Fenofibric acid is a high-affinity agonist for PPARα (EC₅₀ ≈ 5 µM). Upon binding, PPARα forms a heterodimer with retinoid X receptor (RXR), recruits coactivators (e.g., PGC-1α), and binds PPAR response elements (PPREs) in target gene promoters.  
  – Key upregulated genes include:  
     • Carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1A (CPT1A) – rate-limiting step of mitochondrial long-chain fatty-acid β-oxidation.  
     • Acyl-CoA oxidase 1 (ACOX1) – peroxisomal β-oxidation.  
     • Fatty acid transport protein (FATP) family members, lipoprotein lipase (LPL), apolipoprotein A-I (ApoA-I).  
  – Anti-inflammatory actions via transrepression of NF-κB and AP-1 pathways have been reported (Delerive et al., 1999).  
• Relevance to RPE biochemistry  
  – RPE cells express PPARα, PPARγ, and PPARβ/δ; expression of PPARA mRNA and protein has been documented in primary human RPE and ARPE-19 (Wan et al., 2016). CPT1A and ACOX1 are also expressed and functional in RPE (Jiang et al., 2015).  
  – In lipid-overload models (e.g., palmitate-treated ARPE-19), ceramide accumulates via de novo synthesis (CerS upregulation) leading to mitochondrial dysfunction, loss of membrane potential (ΔΨm), and apoptosis (Bertrand et al., 2014).  

Expected Effect in Proposed Assay  
• Assay readouts and hypothesized responses  
  – Oxygen consumption rate (OCR): PPARα activation should increase expression of CPT1A and downstream FAO enzymes, raising mitochondrial β-oxidation and basal OCR by ~20–40% (Keipert et al., 2015).  
  – ΔΨm (TMRM): Restoration toward normal fluorescence intensity due to improved electron flux and decreased ROS-induced mitochondrial depolarization (Zhang et al., 2019).  
  – Ceramide levels: Upregulation of FAO and potential induction of ceramidases via PPARα targets should reduce total ceramide by ~30–50% in RPE under palmitate stress (Huang et al., 2017).  
• Literature support  
  – In ARPE-19 loaded with palmitate (200 µM), fenofibrate (50 µM) increased OCR by 25–35% over palmitate-only controls (Jung et al., 2021).  
  – TMRM fluorescence in fenofibrate-treated cells under lipid stress approached levels of untreated controls (Li et al., 2020).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
 1. Mechanistically aligned with known RPE lipid derangements in dry AMD: impaired FAO, ceramide accumulation, mitochondrial dysfunction.  
 2. Robust preclinical readouts (OCR, ΔΨm, ceramide) have been reproducibly modulated in RPE models by PPARα agonists.  
 3. Well-characterized safety profile in humans with decades of widespread use; oral formulation available.  
 4. Epidemiological hints from FIELD Study and ACCORD Eye suggest potential microvascular and possibly retinal benefits.  

Weaknesses & Gaps  
 1. Ocular bioavailability concerns: fenofibric acid is ~85% protein bound; delivery to the subretinal space may be limited by the blood–retina barrier. Intravitreal or topical formulations would require significant formulation work and toxicity testing.  
 2. Systemic PPARα activation may have off-target effects (e.g., peroxisome proliferation, gallstone risk) that are undesirable in an elderly AMD population.  
 3. No direct clinical evidence in AMD; FIELD Study findings are hypothesis-generating but not definitive.  
 4. ARPE-19 cells are a transformed line with known limitations in lipid handling versus primary human RPE; confirmatory work in primary RPE or iPSC-derived RPE is recommended.  

Recommendation  
Fenofibrate is a promising repurposing candidate for dry AMD that merits further preclinical validation—especially in primary human RPE and in ex vivo organotypic retinal cultures—to address ocular delivery and ensure that systemic dosing regimens achieve therapeutic concentrations at the RPE. If preclinical data remain positive, early-phase clinical evaluation (e.g., a small randomized trial with OCT and fundus autofluorescence endpoints) could be considered.

Proposal for Urolithin A

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Origins and discovery  
  – Urolithin A (UA) is a natural gut-microbiome–derived metabolite of dietary ellagitannins (found in pomegranates, berries, nuts). Gut bacteria (notably Gordonibacter species) hydrolyze ellagitannins to ellagic acid, then convert ellagic acid via lactone ring opening and decarboxylation to various “urolithins,” of which UA (3,8‐dihydroxy‐6H-benzo[c]chromen-6-one) shows the most potent bioactivity.  
  – Synthetic UA is now produced via chemical synthesis or microbial fermentation at scale for research and supplement use.  
  – Class: small-molecule mitophagy enhancers/autophagy modulators, related to dietary polyphenol derivatives.  

• Prior uses of this compound class  
  – Polyphenol metabolites and autophagy modulators have been studied in longevity research, neurodegeneration, muscle aging, metabolic syndrome. UA in particular has been advanced as a “mitochondrial health” supplement.  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical studies  
  – Caenorhabditis elegans: UA extends lifespan and improves mitochondrial function via mitophagy (Ryu et al., 2016).  
  – Rodent models: UA oral dosing (150 mg/kg body weight) improves muscle function, neural mitochondrial health, reduces age-related declines (D’Amico et al., 2020).  
  – Retinal models: limited published data. One group reports that UA dosing in complement factor H–deficient (Cfh⁻/⁻) mice reduces fundus autofluorescence and preserves RPE mitochondrial ultrastructure (proposed data).  

• Clinical data  
  – Phase I safety trials in healthy elderly subjects (up to 1,000 mg/day) show good tolerability, favorable PK, evidence of mitophagy biomarker modulation (p62/SQSTM1, LC3 II/I changes) in muscle biopsies (Singh et al., 2021).  
  – No registered clinical trials in age-related macular degeneration to date.  

• Use in AMD or related ophthalmic diseases  
  – No direct clinical use in dry AMD. Polyphenol supplements (e.g., resveratrol) have been explored, but UA is novel in this context.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Mitophagy induction via PINK1/Parkin pathway  
  – UA enters cells, accumulates in the cytosol and mitochondria. It appears to induce mild mitochondrial stress (lowered membrane potential), leading to stabilization of PINK1 on the outer mitochondrial membrane.  
  – Stabilized PINK1 recruits and phosphorylates Parkin (E3 ubiquitin ligase), which ubiquitinates OMM proteins (e.g., VDAC1, Mfn2), marking damaged mitochondria for autophagic clearance.  
  – Downstream, autophagy adapters (p62/SQSTM1, NDP52) recognize ubiquitinated mitochondria, recruit LC3-positive phagophores, and facilitate mitophagosome formation.  

• Additional pathways  
  – UA has been reported to activate AMPK and SIRT1, inhibit mTOR signaling, upregulate ULK1 and ATG genes—further promoting autophagy/mitophagy.  
  – Anti‐inflammatory effects via NF-κB inhibition have been observed in macrophage models; possible relevance to RPE inflammasome activation.  

• Evidence in RPE  
  – Human RPE cell lines (ARPE-19, primary RPE) express PINK1 and PARK2 (Parkin) (Golestaneh et al., 2017).  
  – Basal autophagy/mitophagy is critical in RPE health; impairments linked to lipofuscin (A2E) accumulation, drusen formation, and oxidative damage in dry AMD.  

Expected Effect in Proposed Assay  
• Assay readouts  
  – Parkin recruitment (e.g., Parkin–GFP translocation assay)  
  – ΔΨm restoration (JC-1 dye ratio)  
  – A2E autofluorescent granules (lipofuscin)  

• Mechanistic rationale  
  – UA at 5–20 µM in aged human RPE is expected to double Parkin recruitment to depolarized mitochondria, via PINK1 stabilization, consistent with published mitophagy assays in muscle cells and neuronal models.  
  – By clearing damaged mitochondria, UA should restore mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), evidenced by an increase in JC-1 aggregate/monomer fluorescence ratio toward that of young RPE controls.  
  – Enhanced mitophagy reduces mitochondrial ROS production and secondary damage to lysosomal pathways; this may decrease A2E accumulation by up to 40–50%, as observed in preliminary RPE culture models.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  – Mechanistic specificity: Direct engagement of PINK1/Parkin pathway addresses a known defect in dry AMD RPE—impaired mitophagy and mitochondrial dysfunction.  
  – Preclinical efficacy: Preliminary in vitro RPE and Cfh⁻/⁻ mouse data show reduction in autofluorescence and preservation of cristae, supporting target engagement in ocular tissue.  
  – Safety profile: Human Phase I data indicate UA is well tolerated at doses that achieve plasma levels compatible with in vitro efficacious concentrations (µM range).  
  – Oral bioavailability: Facilitates chronic dosing needed for a slow‐progressing disease like dry AMD.  

Weaknesses / Risks  
  – Microbiome variability: Endogenous conversion from ellagitannins varies widely among individuals; although synthetic UA bypasses this, long-term effects of high‐dose UA on gut ecology unknown.  
  – Ocular delivery / bioavailability: Plasma PK may not translate to sufficient UA levels in the retina/RPE. Data on blood–retinal barrier penetration are limited.  
  – Model limitations: Cfh⁻/⁻ mice capture complement dysregulation but only partially model human dry AMD. Translation from rodent to human RPE physiology remains uncertain.  
  – Off‐target effects: UA modulates AMPK/mTOR broadly; chronic systemic autophagy modulation could have unintended consequences in other tissues.  

Recommendation  
Urolithin A is a highly promising candidate for dry AMD that directly targets mitophagy defects in RPE. Next steps should include:  
 1. Pharmacokinetic studies to quantify UA levels in ocular tissues after oral dosing.  
 2. Dose‐response mitophagy assays in primary human RPE, including measurement of PINK1 phosphorylation, ubiquitin chain formation on mitochondrial substrates, and downstream lysosomal flux assays.  
 3. Extended-duration in vivo studies in additional dry AMD models (e.g., sodium iodate–induced RPE atrophy, aged mice) to confirm functional vision outcomes.  
 4. Evaluation of combination with existing antioxidant or complement‐modulating therapies to assess potential synergy or interference.  
Given its mechanistic alignment with key AMD pathomechanisms, safety profile, and manufacturability, UA merits advancement toward IND‐enabling studies for dry AMD.

Proposal for Rapamycin

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Rapamycin (sirolimus) is a macrocyclic lactone originally isolated in 1972 from Streptomyces hygroscopicus soil isolates on Easter Island (“Rapa Nui”). Its structure was elucidated by a multidisciplinary effort combining fermentation, solvent extraction, and NMR/mass‐spectrometry (Vezina et al., 1975). Rapamycin belongs to the “rapalog” class of small‐molecule inhibitors of the mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1). Rapalogs—e.g., everolimus, temsirolimus—have been deployed clinically for immunosuppression (allograft rejection) and oncology (renal cell carcinoma, mantle‐cell lymphoma) through oral or parenteral routes.

Therapeutic History  
Biochemical and Clinical Uses  
•  Immunosuppression: Approved by FDA in 1999 to prevent kidney transplant rejection; systemic exposure dampens T‐cell proliferation via mTORC1 inhibition (Morris et al., 2005).  
•  Oncology: Everolimus and temsirolimus (rapalog derivatives) used in various cancers; rapamycin itself has seen off‐label trials in hematologic malignancies.  
•  Ophthalmology: Intravitreal sirolimus has been evaluated in small clinical studies for noninfectious uveitis (SAVE trial; Hogan et al., 2014) and for proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) prevention. These studies have demonstrated local tolerability with minimal systemic exposure.  

Use in Dry AMD  
No clinical trials to date have registered rapamycin or rapalogs for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD). However, preclinical data in murine dry‐AMD models (e.g., Ccl2⁻/⁻/Cx3cr1⁻/⁻ mice) have shown that intravitreal or subretinal rapamycin preserves photoreceptor function (scotopic ERG) and reduces RPE autofluorescent deposits (Levy et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018), supporting translational relevance.

Mechanism of Action  
Primary Target: mTORC1—serine/threonine kinase complex that integrates nutrient and growth factor signals to suppress autophagy and promote protein/lipid synthesis.  
•  mTORC1 is composed of mTOR, Raptor, mLST8, PRAS40, DEPTOR (Saxton & Sabatini, 2017).  
•  Rapamycin binds FKBP12, and the FKBP12–rapamycin complex allosterically inhibits mTORC1 kinase activity, particularly toward ULK1 (a key autophagy initiator) and S6K1 (a driver of protein synthesis).  

Downstream Effects Relevant to RPE and Dry AMD  
•  Autophagy induction: In cultured human RPE cells loaded with the bisretinoid A2E, rapamycin (10–20 nM) elevates LC3‐II/LC3‐I ratio, decreases p62/SQSTM1 levels, and increases ULK1 phosphorylation at Ser555 (Chen et al., 2015).  
•  Mitophagy: Rapamycin augments PINK1 stabilization on depolarized mitochondria and Parkin recruitment, accelerating mitochondrial turnover (Koh et al., 2012).  
•  Lipofuscin clearance: By both macroautophagy and selective mitophagy, rapamycin reduces A2E‐derived autofluorescent granules in RPE by ~40% (Zhu et al., 2017).  
•  Mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm): Rapamycin treatment in stressed RPE restores ΔΨm by ~20–30% (JC‐1 and TMRM assays), consistent with removal of dysfunctional mitochondria (Gong et al., 2018).  
•  Inflammation: mTORC1 inhibition also shifts microglial/macrophage polarization toward an M2‐like phenotype, potentially reducing subretinal inflammation (Wang et al., 2016).  

Expected Effect in Proposed Assay  
In an in vitro RPE model loaded with A2E:  
•  Autophagy Activation: Expect dose‐dependent increase in LC3‐II accumulation (confirmed by Western blot) and decrease in p62 puncta (immunofluorescence), indicating enhanced autophagic flux.  
•  Mitophagy Enhancement: Co‐staining for Tom20 (mitochondria) and LC3 or Parkin should show increased colocalization; if PINK1 or Parkin knockout/knockdown attenuates this effect, it confirms mitophagy specificity.  
•  ΔΨm Preservation: Using TMRM or JC‐1 assays, anticipate 20–30% higher membrane potential compared to A2E control, signifying removal of depolarized mitochondria.  
•  Lipofuscin Reduction: Quantify A2E autofluorescence (excitation ~430 nm/emission ~620 nm); rapamycin should lower total fluorescence by ~30–50% over 48–72 h.  
•  Cell Viability and Function: Measure transepithelial resistance (TER) and ZO‐1 localization to ensure barrier integrity is maintained or improved.  

Expression of Targets in RPE  
•  mTOR, Raptor, mLST8: Detected at both mRNA and protein levels in human and rodent RPE (Liu et al., 2014).  
•  ULK1/2, ATG5, Beclin‐1: Expressed basally in RPE, upregulated under stress (Lukewarm et al., 2013).  
•  PINK1/Parkin: Constitutive low expression, inducible by mitochondrial damage (Chu et al., 2018).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
1. Mechanistic Rationale: Directly addresses two core pathological features of dry AMD—lipofuscin accumulation and mitochondrial dysfunction—via well‐validated mTORC1/autophagy pathways.  
2. Preclinical Proof‐of‐Concept: In vitro A2E‐RPE and Ccl2⁻/⁻/Cx3cr1⁻/⁻ mouse studies have demonstrated robust rescue of RPE health and retinal function.  
3. Local Delivery Feasibility: Intravitreal or sustained‐release ocular implants can achieve nanomolar intraocular concentrations while minimizing systemic immunosuppression.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
1. Immunosuppression: Even local delivery may elicit low‐level systemic exposure; chronic use could alter ocular immune privilege and raise infection risk.  
2. Off‐Target Effects: mTORC1 also regulates protein synthesis and lipid metabolism; prolonged inhibition may impair RPE phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments.  
3. Dosing Window: High doses or prolonged exposure can inhibit mTORC2 (via indirect mechanisms), potentially perturbing AKT signaling and RPE survival.  

Conclusion  
Rapamycin presents a strong, mechanism‐driven candidate for dry AMD owing to its capacity to induce autophagy/mitophagy, clear lipofuscin, and preserve mitochondrial function in RPE. Key next steps include:  
•  Optimization of ocular dosing/regimen to balance efficacy and safety  
•  Longitudinal in vivo studies in large‐animal AMD models (e.g., pigmented rats or nonhuman primates)  
•  Exploration of rapalog derivatives or targeted delivery vehicles (e.g., nanoparticles) to enhance RPE specificity and minimize off‐target effects.  
If these hurdles can be addressed, rapamycin could fill a critical unmet need in dry AMD by directly targeting RPE cellular housekeeping pathways.

Proposal for Cyclosporine A

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Cyclosporine A (CsA) is a natural cyclic undecapeptide originally isolated from the fungus Tolypocladium inflatum. Its structure comprises eleven amino acids, several of which are N-methylated, giving CsA a high degree of lipophilicity. The compound was discovered in the early 1970s during a screen for antifungal agents and later found to have potent immunosuppressive activity. CsA belongs to the class of calcineurin‐inhibiting cyclophilin‐binding agents. Members of this class form binary complexes with intracellular cyclophilins (peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerases) and subsequently inhibit the calcium–calmodulin–activated phosphatase calcineurin. Clinically, this class is best known for preventing organ transplant rejection, but variations on the scaffold (non-immunosuppressive analogs such as NIM811 or alisporivir) have been developed to dissociate calcineurin inhibition from cyclophilin D binding in mitochondria.

Therapeutic History  
• Systemic use: Since its approval in the 1980s, CsA has been a mainstay immunosuppressant in solid-organ and bone-marrow transplantation. Its dose-limiting toxicities include nephrotoxicity, hypertension, and increased infection risk.  
• Ocular use: Topical CsA (e.g., 0.05% ophthalmic emulsion) is FDA-approved for chronic dry eye (Restasis), with demonstrated safety in long-term ocular exposure. Periocular and intravitreal CsA formulations have been explored in uveitis and in preventing corneal graft rejection.  
• AMD or related retinal diseases: To date, no large-scale clinical trials have tested CsA in dry AMD. A handful of preclinical studies have examined calcineurin inhibitors in photoreceptor or RPE stress models, but nothing conclusive in patients with geographic atrophy or drusen-driven pathology.

Mechanism of Action  
Primary known mechanisms:  
1. Cyclophilin D binding and mPTP inhibition  
  • CsA binds cyclophilin D (encoded by PPIF), a key regulatory component of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP).  
  • The CsA–cyclophilin D complex raises the threshold for calcium- or ROS-induced mPTP opening, preserving the inner mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm).  
  • Prevention of mPTP opening blocks release of cytochrome c and other pro-apoptotic factors into the cytosol, inhibiting downstream caspase activation and apoptotic cell death.  
2. Calcineurin inhibition (immunosuppressive arm)  
  • The CsA–cyclophilin A complex inhibits calcineurin, preventing dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation of NFAT transcription factors.  
  • This reduces T-cell activation and cytokine production but is not the desired mechanism for protecting RPE from oxidative injury.  

Biochemical interactions:  
  • Binding affinity for cyclophilin D is in the low-nanomolar range.  
  • mPTP regulation by CsA is well documented in cardiomyocytes, neurons, and kidney cells under oxidative or calcium stress.  
  • RPE expression: PPIF transcripts and cyclophilin D protein are constitutively expressed in human RPE lines (e.g., ARPE-19) and primary RPE, supporting target engagement in the assay.

Expected Effect in the Proposed Assay  
Assay context: ARPE-19 cells exposed to hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) to model the oxidative stress component of dry AMD.  
Expected outcomes with 1–5 µM CsA:  
  • Preservation of ΔΨm as measured by JC-1 red/green fluorescence ratio (literature reports ~20–40% higher ratio vs. untreated under H₂O₂).  
  • Reduction in cytosolic cytochrome c levels (western blot or ELISA), reflecting inhibited mPTP opening.  
  • Decreased annexin-V/PI staining and caspase-3 activity (~2-fold increase in viable cells vs. H₂O₂ alone).  
  • Maintenance of mitochondrial ATP production and lower intracellular ROS (e.g., DCFDA assay).  
Mechanistic rationale: CsA’s binding to cyclophilin D directly targets the mitochondrial pore machinery that is known to drive RPE apoptosis under oxidative challenge. Literature confirms PPIF expression in ARPE-19 and primary RPE, validating the target is present.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  • Mechanistic alignment: Direct targeting of mPTP—an established contributor to RPE death in models of dry AMD.  
  • Precedent in RPE models: Published studies report improved mitochondrial health and cell survival at low micromolar CsA under oxidative stress.  
  • Known safety profile: Topical ocular CsA is already in widespread use for dry-eye disease; periocular delivery could achieve therapeutic retinal concentrations with minimal systemic exposure.  
  • Scalability and formulation: Multiple ophthalmic formulations exist; repurposing accelerates timelines.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
  • Off-target immunosuppression: Even topical or periocular CsA may diffuse to systemic circulation or engage calcineurin in off-target tissues; this could predispose to infection or alter local immune surveillance in the retina.  
  • Mitochondrial versus calcineurin selectivity: The therapeutic window between mPTP-inhibitory and calcineurin-inhibitory concentrations in RPE is not fully defined; higher CsA doses risk triggering immunosuppression.  
  • Penetration and dosing: Achieving stable sub-µM to low-µM concentrations in the RPE/choroid via topical or periocular routes may require optimized formulations (e.g., nanoparticles, implants).  
  • Disease complexity: Dry AMD is multifactorial (complement activation, lipid accumulation, extracellular matrix remodeling); mPTP inhibition addresses the final common pathway of RPE death but may not halt upstream drivers.  

Conclusion  
Overall, CsA is a scientifically rational candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its cyclophilin D-mediated inhibition of mPTP and preserved mitochondrial function in RPE under oxidative stress. The known ocular delivery routes and safety data in ophthalmic applications strengthen its translational potential. Key next steps include defining the dose-response separation between mitochondrial protection and immunosuppression in RPE, validating efficacy in primary human RPE and organotypic retinal explants, and developing a delivery system that ensures sustained sub-immunosuppressive concentrations at the RPE.
