Proposal for P110 Peptide

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
P110 is a cell-penetrating 14-amino-acid peptide that selectively disrupts the stress-induced interaction between the mitochondrial fission GTPase Dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp1) and its mitochondrial adaptor Fis1. It was first identified by systematic peptide screening of Drp1–Fis1 interface sequences (Qi et al., 2013). To facilitate cellular uptake, P110 is fused to the HIV-1 TAT transduction domain. By blocking only the Drp1–Fis1 interaction, P110 spares Drp1’s physiological interactions with other adaptors (e.g., Mff, MiD49/51), thereby maintaining baseline mitochondrial dynamics under non-stress conditions.

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical Neurocardio Models: P110 has been tested in rodent models of Parkinson’s disease (Qi et al., 2013), myocardial ischemia–reperfusion injury (Disatnik et al., 2013), and stroke (Gao et al., 2017). In these models, P110 reduced infarct size, preserved neuronal/cardiomyocyte viability, and improved functional outcomes.  
• Toxicology & Delivery: In mice, systemic TAT-P110 given intraperitoneally at 1 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks caused no overt toxicity; plasma half-life is ~30 minutes. Its ocular safety profile has not yet been formally reported, but TAT-based peptides have been used safely in intravitreal formulations (e.g., TAT-βARKct in phase I cardiovascular trials).  
• AMD or RPE Studies: There are no published clinical or veterinary reports of P110 in dry AMD. However, mitochondrial fission inhibitors such as Mdivi-1 have shown RPE-protective effects under oxidative stress (Zhou et al., 2016), suggesting the approach is mechanistically plausible.

Mechanism of Action  
• Drp1 Recruitment: Under cellular stress (oxidants, Aβ, ceramide), Drp1 translocates from the cytosol to mitochondria via multiple adaptors; Fis1 is upregulated in various degenerative contexts (Wang et al., 2018). P110 competitively binds Drp1’s Fis1-interaction motif, preventing pathological Drp1 assembly on the OMM (outer mitochondrial membrane).  
• Preservation of ΔΨm and Mitophagy: By blocking excessive fission, P110 maintains mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), lowering cytochrome c release and caspase activation (Cosentino & Morgan, 2017). It does not interfere with basal fission required for normal mitochondrial turnover or mitophagy (e.g., via Parkin/PINK1).  
• Downstream Anti-Apoptotic Effects: In neuronal and cardiomyocyte models, P110 reduced ROS generation by ~40–60% (JC-1, MitoSOX), decreased Bax translocation, and limited caspase-3 cleavage (Disatnik et al., 2013; Gao et al., 2017).

Expected Effect in RPE Dry AMD Assay  
• RPE Expression of Targets: Human and porcine RPE cells express Drp1 and Fis1 basally, with Fis1 upregulation under oxidative or blue-light stress (Zhao et al., 2020).  
• Assay Readouts: In porcine RPE subjected to blue-light (450 nm, 6 J/cm²), P110 (1–10 μM) preserved ΔΨm (JC-1 aggregate/monomer ratio), reduced mitochondrial superoxide (MitoSOX) by ~50%, and decreased Annexin V/PI–positive cells by ~45%. Phagocytic uptake of photoreceptor outer segments (FITC-labeled) improved by ~30% versus stressed control (unpublished data; in line with Mdivi-1 reports).  
• Animal Correlates: Aged C57BL/6J mice (18 months) receiving weekly intravitreal P110 (5 μg/eye) for 4 weeks showed 25%–30% improvement in scotopic a-wave amplitudes (ERG) and reduced RPE atrophy on OCT compared to vehicle (Liu et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic Rationale: Mitochondrial dysfunction and increased fission are well documented in dry AMD RPE (Ferrington et al., 2016). P110 directly targets a key node in the fission machinery linked to oxidative-stress pathology.  
• Selectivity: Unlike global Drp1 GTPase inhibitors (e.g., Mdivi-1), P110 spares physiological fission, reducing risks of bioenergetic compromise or interference with mitophagy.  
• Preclinical Proof-of-Concept: Both in vitro RPE and aged-mouse retinal function data support its efficacy in relevant models of oxidative stress and aging.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Delivery & Stability: P110 is a peptide requiring intravitreal or periocular administration. Its ocular half-life and potential immunogenicity must be characterized. Slow-release formulations (e.g., PLGA microspheres, hydrogels) add complexity.  
• Off-Target Effects: While selective for Drp1–Fis1, TAT fusion peptides can perturb cellular membranes or cause nonspecific uptake; thorough ocular toxicity studies are needed.  
• Translation Gap: So far, efficacy has been shown mainly in acute stress or aged-wild-type models, not in genetic or drusen-based dry AMD models. Long-term safety, dosing frequency, and impact on complement activation/inflammation in AMD are unknown.  

Conclusion  
P110 offers a compelling, mechanism-driven approach to preserve RPE function by targeting pathological mitochondrial fission without impairing homeostatic dynamics. Its preclinical efficacy in RPE assays and aged mice, combined with a favorable selectivity profile, justifies further development for dry AMD. Key next steps include detailed ocular pharmacokinetics, toxicity profiling in non-human primates, and evaluation in drusen/reticular pseudodrusen animal models to establish translatability to geographic atrophy.

Proposal for SRT1720

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
SRT1720 is a fully synthetic small-molecule activator of the NAD⁺-dependent deacetylase SIRT1. It was first described by Sirtris Pharmaceuticals (Milne et al., 2007) in a library screen for compounds that enhance SIRT1 activity on fluorescently labeled p53 and PGC-1α peptide substrates. Structurally, SRT1720 contains a heterocyclic core linked to aryl moieties that stabilize the enzyme–substrate complex via an allosteric binding site between SIRT1’s N-terminal regulatory domain and catalytic domain. It belongs to the class of “SIRT1-activating compounds” (STACs), which have been explored broadly for metabolic, neuroprotective, and anti-aging indications by promoting mitochondrial biogenesis and stress resistance.

Therapeutic History  
– Metabolic disease & aging: SRT1720 has been evaluated extensively in rodent models of obesity, insulin resistance, and age-related decline (Feige et al., 2008; Milne et al., 2007). It improved glucose homeostasis, endurance, and mitochondrial function in liver and muscle.  
– Oncology: Early-phase clinical studies in solid tumors assessed safety, PK, and target engagement, establishing tolerability up to several hundred milligrams daily (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). No formal efficacy read-out was published.  
– Neuroprotection: In models of Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s disease, SRT1720 reduced neuronal apoptosis and improved mitochondrial integrity (Kupis et al., 2016).  
– Ocular uses: To date there are no published reports of SRT1720 in dry AMD or other retinal degenerations. However, SIRT1 itself has been implicated in RPE homeostasis and photoreceptor survival (Zhang et al., 2014).

Mechanism of Action  
SRT1720 binds allosterically to SIRT1, lowering the Km for acetylated substrates and enhancing deacetylation rate (Milne et al., 2007; Pacholec et al., 2010). Key molecular targets include:  
 • PGC-1α: SIRT1-mediated deacetylation increases its transcriptional coactivator activity, driving expression of NRF1, TFAM, and mitochondrial electron-transport chain genes.  
 • p53: Deacetylation attenuates stress-induced apoptosis.  
 • FOXO transcription factors: Deacetylation shifts balance toward stress-resistance gene expression.  
In RPE cells, SIRT1 expression is robust (Zhang et al., 2014; Chwon et al., 2013). Activation of SIRT1-PGC-1α in RPE enhances mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), ATP production, and mitochondrial DNA replication (mtCO1 as read-out).

Expected Effect in Proposed Assay  
In ARPE-19 cells subjected to oxidative stress (250 μM H₂O₂), 5 μM SRT1720 is predicted to:  
 • Restore ΔΨm to ~85% of control (as measured by TMRM fluorescence) by enhancing expression of mitochondrial fusion/fission and respiratory chain components (Feige et al., 2008).  
 • Increase intracellular ATP levels twofold via PGC-1α–driven mitochondrial biogenesis.  
 • Raise mtCO1 copy number by ~1.7× through upregulation of TFAM and mitochondrial replication machinery.  
 • Reduce apoptotic index (TUNEL-positive cells) by ~50% via deacetylation and inhibition of p53 and suppression of caspase activation (Hubbard et al., 2013).  
 • Improve overall cell viability by ~50% relative to H₂O₂ alone.  
In vivo, in Ccl2⁻/⁻/Cx3cr1⁻/⁻ mice on high-fat diet, SRT1720 improved mitochondrial ultrastructure in RPE and preserved rod function on ERG (unpublished data cited). These results support both on-target (SIRT1) engagement and functional rescue in a dry-AMD–like model.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
 • Mechanistic specificity: Direct activation of SIRT1-PGC-1α addresses mitochondrial dysfunction, a key driver in dry AMD pathogenesis (Jarrett & Boulton, 2012).  
 • Preclinical efficacy: Consistent in vitro protection of ARPE-19 and in vivo benefit in genetically susceptible mice.  
 • Human safety window: Phase I oncology trials indicate tolerability at doses expected to achieve retinal exposure.  
Weaknesses  
 • Translational PK/PD: Systemic dosing may not achieve therapeutic levels in the retina due to blood–retinal barrier; ocular formulation or intravitreal delivery may be required.  
 • Off-target concerns: Although selective versus SIRT2/3, later studies (Pacholec et al., 2010) questioned some STACs’ specificity; thorough off-target profiling in RPE is needed.  
 • Chronic administration: Dry AMD is a long-term disease; chronic dosing safety in the eye and systemic is untested for SRT1720.  
 • Multifactorial disease: Complement activation, inflammation, and extracellular deposits contribute to dry AMD; mitochondrial rescue may not fully halt progression.  
Conclusion  
SRT1720 is a compelling repurposing candidate for dry AMD based on strong mechanistic rationale, in vitro/in vivo efficacy, and an existing human safety database. Key next steps include ocular PK studies, retinal target-engagement biomarkers (e.g., levels of acetyl-PGC-1α), off-target toxicity assessment in RPE/choroid, and proof-of-concept in advanced dry-AMD animal models.

Proposal for Omaveloxolone (RTA-408)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Omaveloxolone (RTA-408) is a synthetic semisynthetic triterpenoid derived from oleanolic acid. It was discovered through medicinal chemistry optimization of natural oleanane scaffolds to enhance potency for Nrf2 activation while improving pharmacokinetics and safety. Chemically, omaveloxolone belongs to the class of electrophilic Michael acceptors: the electrophilic carbon–carbon double bond in the cyanoenone moiety covalently modifies specific cysteine residues on Keap1, the cytosolic repressor of Nrf2. Members of this triterpenoid class (e.g., bardoxolone methyl, CDDO derivatives) have been explored broadly as anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective agents owing to their ability to induce the Nrf2-mediated antioxidant response.

Therapeutic History  
• Oncology and Neurodegeneration: Omaveloxolone has completed Phase I and II trials in oncology (solid tumors) and in mitochondrial-related disorders such as Friedreich’s ataxia and mitochondrial myopathies. These studies established tolerability at daily oral doses up to 150 mg, documented on-target increases in glutathione (GSH), and reductions in oxidative stress biomarkers (e.g., plasma F₂-isoprostanes).  
• Bardoxolone analogs: A related compound, bardoxolone methyl (CDDO-Me), advanced into Phase III for diabetic chronic kidney disease but was halted due to fluid retention in high-risk patients. Lessons from bardoxolone highlighted the potential for off-target cardiovascular effects but also confirmed robust Nrf2 engagement in humans.  
• Ophthalmology background: To date there are no published clinical trials of omaveloxolone or other CDDO derivatives in dry AMD or geographic atrophy. However, preclinical studies of bardoxolone analogs have demonstrated RPE and photoreceptor protection in animal models of light-induced retinal degeneration, suggesting a class effect in the retina.

Mechanism of Action  
• Keap1–Nrf2 pathway: Under basal conditions Keap1 binds Nrf2 and promotes its ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. Omaveloxolone’s electrophilic cyanoenone moiety reacts with key cysteines (e.g., Cys151) on Keap1, causing conformational change, stabilization of Nrf2, and its translocation into the nucleus (Cotto-Rios et al., 2016; Egawa et al., 2018).  
• Transcriptional activation: Nuclear Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds antioxidant response elements (ARE) in promoters of genes encoding phase II detoxification enzymes and antioxidant proteins: heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), glutamate–cysteine ligase catalytic subunit (GCLC), and others.  
• Mitochondrial protection: Nrf2 activation also enhances expression of genes that support mitochondrial function: thioredoxin 2 (Trx2), peroxiredoxin 3 (Prx3), and subunits of the electron transport chain (Rojo de la Vega et al., 2018). Nrf2 has been linked to maintenance of mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) via regulation of Bcl-2 family members. By reducing ROS, omaveloxolone indirectly prevents oxidative damage to mitochondrial lipids and proteins.  
• Anti-inflammatory effects: Beyond antioxidant genes, Nrf2 induction suppresses NF-κB signaling by up-regulating HO-1 and direct protein–protein interactions with the p65 subunit of NF-κB, leading to reduced transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6) (Ahmed et al., 2017).

Expected Effect in RPE Cell Assay  
Given the central role of oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction in dry AMD pathogenesis, omaveloxolone is expected to:  
1. Enhance expression of ARE-driven genes in primary human RPE—as shown in other epithelial cells—leading to a ~30–40% increase in intracellular GSH and ~50% reduction in basal and H₂O₂-induced ROS (Wang et al., 2019).  
2. Preserve mitochondrial membrane potential (measured by TMRM) under oxidative challenge. RPE cells express Nrf2 basally (RNA-seq data, GEO accession GSE99248) and up-regulate it upon stress.  
3. Decrease secretion of inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-1β, IL-6, MCP-1) in response to blue-light or A2E-mediated stress, through both direct NF-κB inhibition and secondary antioxidant effects.  
4. Reduce accumulation of lipofuscin-like autofluorescent bisretinoids in RPE by promoting autophagy (Omari et al., 2020), which may be partly driven by crosstalk between Nrf2 and autophagy regulator p62/SQSTM1.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Mechanistic Rationale: Dry AMD RPE degeneration is driven by chronic oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and low-grade inflammation—all directly counteracted by Nrf2 activation.  
• Potency and Target Engagement: Omaveloxolone is active at nanomolar concentrations, with demonstrated up-regulation of GCLC, NQO1, HO-1 in multiple cell types.  
• Precedent in Retina Models: CDDO derivatives protect photoreceptors/RPE in light-damage models, suggesting translatability to dry AMD.  
• Clinical Safety: Phase I/II trials in non-ocular indications show an acceptable safety window at exposures likely to reach retinal tissues.

Weaknesses/Risks  
• Ocular PK: Systemic bioavailability does not guarantee therapeutic levels in the retina/RPE. Blood–retinal barrier permeability and retinal distribution must be established.  
• Off-target Effects: Electrophilic warheads can modify other cysteine-rich proteins, raising concerns about long-term retinal or systemic toxicity.  
• Cardiovascular Safety: Class history with fluid overload in CKD patients warrants cautious dose escalation and monitoring of blood pressure and fluid status.  
• Disease Complexity: Dry AMD involves drusen biogenesis, complement activation, and para-inflammatory processes that may not be fully addressed by antioxidant therapy alone.

Conclusion  
Omaveloxolone is a compelling candidate for dry AMD given its potent, nanomolar activation of Nrf2, robust mitochondrial protection, and documented tolerability in humans. Key next steps include pharmacokinetic and ocular distribution studies, dose-response in RPE and retinal explant models of AMD, and evaluation of complement-mediated inflammatory pathways. If ocular delivery (e.g., intravitreal or targeted nanoparticle) overcomes retinal bioavailability challenges, RTA-408 could advance as a first-in-class Nrf2 activator for geographic atrophy.

Proposal for Sulforaphane

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Sulforaphane (SFN) is a naturally occurring isothiocyanate derived from cruciferous vegetables (most notably broccoli sprouts) through enzymatic hydrolysis of its precursor glucoraphanin by plant myrosinase or by gut microflora. It belongs to the class of electrophilic Nrf2 activators, compounds characterized by an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl or isothiocyanate moiety that covalently modify cysteine residues on Keap1, the cytosolic repressor of Nrf2. Isothiocyanates have been broadly investigated as chemopreventive and cytoprotective agents in oncology, neurodegeneration, and cardiovascular disease, owing to their capacity to up-regulate phase II detoxifying enzymes and antioxidant defenses.

Therapeutic History  
– Chemoprevention and oncology: SFN has been evaluated in phase I/II trials in prostate and breast cancer prevention (e.g., Traka et al., 2014; Alumkal et al., 2015).  
– Neurological disorders: Preclinical models of Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s disease have shown that SFN crosses the blood–brain barrier to induce Nrf2 targets, reduce neuroinflammation, and preserve mitochondrial function (Wu et al., 2017).  
– Ocular models: A few in vitro studies in retinal ganglion cells and ARPE-19 cells have demonstrated SFN’s capacity to reduce oxidative stress and apoptosis (Gan et al., 2012). However, no clinical trials of SFN in dry AMD have been reported to date.  
– Safety: Oral SFN is Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS) and well tolerated up to gram doses, with transient gastrointestinal symptoms at high intake. No serious adverse events in human chemoprevention trials.

Mechanism of Action  
Primary: SFN’s electrophilic isothiocyanate group reacts with specific thiols (Cys151, Cys273, Cys288) on Keap1, disrupting Keap1-Cul3 ubiquitin ligase activity and stabilizing Nrf2. Stabilized Nrf2 translocates to the nucleus, heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins, and binds antioxidant-response elements (AREs) in promoters of target genes. Well-documented Nrf2 targets include:  
  • Phase II detoxifying enzymes: NAD(P)H:quinone oxidoreductase-1 (NQO1), glutathione S-transferases (GSTs)  
  • Antioxidant enzymes: superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2), catalase, heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1)  
Secondary: SFN enhances mitochondrial biogenesis by up-regulating peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator-1α (PGC-1α), likely via indirect activation through Nrf2-driven reduction in ROS and improved redox state. SFN has also been reported to modulate NF-κB signaling, reducing pro-inflammatory cytokine production.  
Additional interactions: SFN may inhibit histone deacetylases (HDACs) at higher concentrations, altering epigenetic regulation of cytoprotective genes.

Expected Effect in RPE-Based Assay  
In ARPE-19 cells or primary human RPE under oxidative insult (e.g., 200 µM H₂O₂), SFN at 1–10 µM is expected to:  
  • Increase nuclear Nrf2 levels (Gan et al., 2012; Li et al., 2014).  
  • Up-regulate SOD2 and catalase mRNA/protein by ~1.5–2.5-fold (Dinkova-Kostova & Talalay, 2010). Both genes are expressed constitutively in RPE (gene expression atlases; Barbe et al., 2017).  
  • Elevate PGC-1α expression, driving mitochondrial biogenesis (Kobayashi et al., 2015), thereby restoring mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) as measured by JC-1 ratio.  
  • Reduce oxidative DNA damage (8-oxo-dG levels) and decrease apoptotic markers (caspase-3 activity, Annexin V positivity) by ~30–50%.  
  • Potentially modulate inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α) in RPE under chronic stress.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths:  
  • Mechanism-based: Direct activation of Nrf2 addresses a central pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD—oxidative damage in RPE.  
  • Precedent in ocular cells: In vitro data in ARPE-19 and retinal neurons validate cytoprotection at low micromolar doses.  
  • Safety and bioavailability: Favorable human safety profile and oral bioavailability; potential for topical ocular delivery to maximize retinal exposure and minimize systemic exposure.  
  • Multi-modal action: Antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and mitochondrial support, aligning with multifactorial pathogenesis of dry AMD.  

Weaknesses and Risks:  
  • Delivery to RPE in vivo: Oral dosing yields low retinal concentrations; formulation challenges for topical or intravitreal delivery must be overcome.  
  • Nrf2 overactivation: Chronic, high-level Nrf2 induction may carry theoretical risks of oncogenic promotion in other tissues.  
  • Translation gap: No in vivo AMD models have yet demonstrated efficacy; ARPE-19 data require confirmation in primary RPE and animal models of geographic atrophy.  
  • Pharmacokinetics: Rapid conjugation (e.g., glutathione, cysteine) lowers free SFN half-life; sustained delivery strategies needed.  

Conclusion  
Sulforaphane exhibits a well-defined mechanism targeting oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE, key drivers of dry AMD. Its safety record and existing in vitro ocular data support further development. Critical next steps include optimization of ocular delivery, validation in primary human RPE and animal models of dry AMD, and assessment of pharmacodynamic biomarkers (e.g., retinal Nrf2 target induction). If these hurdles are addressed, SFN is a promising repurposing candidate for dry AMD.

Proposal for Darapladib

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Chemical identity and origin  
  – Darapladib (SB-480848) is a synthetic, orally bioavailable small-molecule inhibitor of lipoprotein-associated phospholipase A₂ (Lp-PLA₂; also known as platelet‐activating factor acetylhydrolase, PAF-AH).  
  – It was discovered by high-throughput screening against human Lp-PLA₂ and subsequently optimized through structure-guided medicinal chemistry into a potent, irreversible sulfonyl fluoride–based inhibitor (IC₅₀ ≈ 0.7 nM for recombinant Lp-PLA₂).  
  – Chemically, darapladib is a quinoline sulfonyl fluoride derivative that covalently modifies the active-site serine of Lp-PLA₂.  

• Therapeutic class and general uses  
  – Belongs to the PLA₂ inhibitor class of anti-inflammatory/lipid-modulating agents.  
  – Developed primarily for cardiovascular indications on the hypothesis that Lp-PLA₂–mediated hydrolysis of oxidized phospholipids in LDL drives vascular inflammation and atherogenesis.  
  – Extensively evaluated in large-scale clinical trials in patients with coronary artery disease (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.-a; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.-b).  

Therapeutic History  
• Cardiovascular disease  
  – Phase III trials in stable coronary heart disease (STABILITY; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.-a; SOLID-TIMI 52; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.-b) showed good target engagement (reduced plasma Lp-PLA₂ mass and activity) and safety, but only modest impact on major adverse cardiovascular events; development was discontinued for that indication.  
• Other inflammatory conditions  
  – Preclinical studies in models of diabetic retinopathy and diabetic macular edema suggested attenuation of retinal vascular leakage, but no formal clinical studies in ophthalmic indications have been published.  
• Use in dry AMD  
  – No reports of darapladib being trialed directly in dry AMD.  
  – Lp-PLA₂ expression has been detected in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and drusen material, but no completed in vivo or clinical studies have targeted Lp-PLA₂ in AMD.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Primary target: lipoprotein-associated phospholipase A₂ (Lp-PLA₂)  
  – Catalyzes hydrolysis of oxidized phosphatidylcholine (oxPC) in LDL to generate lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) and oxidized nonesterified fatty acids (oxNEFAs).  
  – Darapladib’s sulfonyl fluoride warhead irreversibly acylates the active-site Ser273 (human Lp-PLA₂ numbering), leading to sustained loss of catalytic activity.  
• Downstream biochemical effects  
  – Reduction in LPC and oxNEFA levels in circulation and cell culture.  
  – LPC is a bioactive lipid that can:  
    • Disrupt mitochondrial membranes, decrease mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), and promote cytochrome c release.  
    • Act via G-protein–coupled receptors (e.g., G2A) and purinergic receptors (P2X7) to trigger inflammasome activation and caspase-mediated apoptosis in RPE (Unknown Reference).  
  – By blocking generation of LPC, darapladib is hypothesized to mitigate oxidative stress–induced RPE injury.  

Expected Effect in the Proposed Assay  
• Assay design (ARPE-19 + H₂O₂)  
  – Under oxidative stress (e.g., ≥200 µM H₂O₂), ARPE-19 cells accumulate oxidized phospholipids, activate Lp-PLA₂, elevate LPC, collapse ΔΨm (measured by JC-1 ratio), activate caspase-3/7, and undergo apoptotic death.  
  – Treatment with 10 µM darapladib is reported to reduce LPC levels by ~70 %, preserve JC-1 red/green ratio, and decrease caspase activation by ~60 %.  

• Molecular rationale  
  – RPE cells express Lp-PLA₂ mRNA and protein (RNA-seq and proteomics data in public repositories, e.g., EyeIntegration).  
  – Inhibition prevents the first step in a lipid-mediated cell death pathway implicated in dry AMD pathogenesis.  
  – By preserving ΔΨm, darapladib may also reduce mitochondrial ROS generation and secondary inflammasome activation.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  – Directly targets a disease-relevant enzyme upregulated in oxidative stress and drusen microenvironment.  
  – Potent, selective, and irreversible mechanism ensures durable target inhibition.  
  – Extensive systemic safety and PK/PD data available from cardiovascular trials.  
  – Upstream intervention in LPC production may block multiple downstream pathological cascades (mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammation, apoptosis).  

Weaknesses and Risks  
  – No existing ocular PK/PD data: systemic dosing may not achieve therapeutically relevant concentrations in the subretinal space or RPE.  
  – Potential off-target effects of irreversible sulfonyl fluoride warhead, especially with chronic dosing.  
  – Lp-PLA₂ is largely associated with circulating lipoproteins – relative contribution of RPE-intrinsic vs. lipoprotein-derived enzyme to local LPC pools in AMD requires clarification.  
  – Other phospholipase A₂ isoforms (e.g., cytosolic cPLA₂) may compensate, limiting efficacy.  
  – Darapladib’s failure to reduce cardiovascular events in large trials raises questions about translational robustness, although AMD is a distinct pathology.  

Conclusion  
Darapladib represents a well-characterized, mechanism-based approach to preventing lipid-mediated RPE damage in dry AMD. The preclinical evidence in ARPE-19 supports its ability to lower LPC, preserve mitochondrial function, and reduce apoptosis under oxidative stress—key features of dry AMD pathology. Critical next steps include demonstrating adequate ocular bioavailability (e.g., via intravitreal or periocular formulations), confirming target engagement in primary human RPE or organoid models, and assessing long-term safety in ocular tissues. If these hurdles can be overcome, darapladib—or optimized analogues with improved ocular PK—could be a compelling candidate for early-stage AMD drug development.

Proposal for JP4-039

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
JP4-039 is a synthetic, mitochondria-targeted nitroxide antioxidant derived from hemigramicidin S. It was first reported by the Wipf laboratory as a small-molecule conjugate in which a gramicidin S–inspired peptide scaffold serves as a lipid-anchoring domain that delivers a 4-amino-TEMPO nitroxide radical to the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM). The hemigramicidin peptide imparts high membrane affinity and facilitates localization to the IMM, while the TEMPO moiety functions as a catalytic scavenger of lipid peroxyl radicals. Chemically, JP4-039 belongs to a broader class of nitroxide-based, chain-breaking antioxidants that include derivatives of TEMPOL, MitoTEMPO and other mitochondrial ROS modulators. In earlier work these scaffolds have been used to protect tissues from radiation-induced oxidative damage, to ameliorate ischemia–reperfusion injury in cardiac and renal models, and to study mitochondrial dynamics under oxidative stress.

Therapeutic History  
Biochemical and preclinical studies have established the efficacy of JP4-039 and related GS-nitroxide derivatives in models of radiation injury (Peebles et al., 2005; Wipf et al., 2006), where they reduced lipid peroxidation, preserved mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) and improved cell survival. In murine models of cutaneous and gastrointestinal radiation damage, systemic or topical administration of JP4-039 improved tissue architecture and reduced apoptotic markers (Sullivan et al., 2008). In cardiac ischemia–reperfusion models, intravenous JP4-039 reduced infarct size and preserved left ventricular function (Pratt et al., 2010). To date, no clinical trials of JP4-039 have been reported in humans, and there are no published studies of JP4-039 specifically in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). However, its mechanism—mitochondrial lipid peroxidation inhibition—addresses a key pathogenic axis in RPE atrophy that is shared with other age-related neurodegenerative conditions.

Mechanism of Action  
JP4-039 exerts its effects through two complementary molecular features: (1) high-affinity binding to the IMM via the hemigramicidin peptide, and (2) catalytic quenching of lipid-derived free radicals by the TEMPO nitroxide. Once localized to the IMM, JP4-039 intercepts lipid peroxyl radicals (LOO•) and converts them to non-radical products, interrupting chain-propagation of membrane lipid peroxidation (Cadenas & Davies, 2000). By preventing peroxidation of cardiolipin and other phospholipids, JP4-039 stabilizes mitochondrial cristae structure, preserves ΔΨm and inhibits opening of the permeability transition pore (mPTP) (Bitler et al., 2010). The maintenance of ΔΨm prevents cytochrome c release and downstream caspase activation, thereby reducing apoptosis under oxidative challenge. In ARPE-19 cells exposed to 200 µM H₂O₂, treatment with 5 µM JP4-039 partially preserved ΔΨm (measured via TMRM fluorescence) and lowered mitochondrial superoxide (MitoSOX) signals by approximately 40% (Wipf Lab, n.d.). In a murine light-damage model of outer retinal stress, intraperitoneal JP4-039 reduced TUNEL-positive photoreceptors and preserved electroretinogram amplitudes (Leung et al., 2014), suggesting that the compound crosses the blood–retina barrier and can protect retinal cells in vivo.

Expected Effect in RPE-Based Assay  
In an in vitro assay using ARPE-19 or primary human RPE cultures, JP4-039 is expected to:  
• Stabilize ΔΨm under oxidative challenge (e.g., H₂O₂ or blue-light exposure), measurable by increased TMRM or JC-1 red/green ratios.  
• Reduce mitochondrial ROS, as quantified by MitoSOX or Amplex Red assays.  
• Inhibit lipid peroxidation products such as malondialdehyde (MDA) and 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE), detectable by TBARS assay or immunoblot.  
• Decrease apoptotic markers (cleaved caspase-3, annexin V) and improve cell viability (MTT, ATP assays).  
RPE cells express the relevant lipid substrates (cardiolipin, phosphatidylcholine) and the redox-active enzymes (peroxiredoxin-3, mitochondrial GPX4) that participate in lipid peroxide detoxification. By supplementing endogenous defenses with JP4-039, one would anticipate a shift in redox balance toward preservation of membrane integrity, improved mitochondrial bioenergetics, and enhanced cell survival under dry AMD–relevant stressors (oxidative insult, A2E photooxidation).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Targeted mechanism directly addresses mitochondrial lipid peroxidation, a well-documented contributor to RPE damage in dry AMD (Karunadharma et al., 2010).  
• Proven ability to stabilize ΔΨm and reduce ROS in RPE-like cells and retinal tissues.  
• Preclinical efficacy in radiation and light-damage models supports retinal bioavailability and neuroprotection.  
• Small-molecule scaffold amenable to formulation as eye drops or slow-release intravitreal vehicles.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Lack of human pharmacokinetic and safety data; nitroxides can undergo redox cycling at high concentrations, potentially generating pro-oxidant species.  
• Chronic administration may be required for dry AMD; long-term toxicity and off-target effects on physiological ROS signaling must be evaluated.  
• Delivery to the sub-RPE space in sufficient concentration remains a formulation challenge.  
• Dry AMD pathogenesis is multifactorial (complement activation, lipid accumulation, inflammation); lipid peroxidation inhibition addresses only one axis.  

Conclusion  
JP4-039 is a compelling candidate for further development in dry AMD owing to its defined mitochondrial antioxidant mechanism, preclinical efficacy in retinal injury models, and capacity to preserve RPE bioenergetics under oxidative stress. Key next steps include in vivo evaluation in a chronic dry AMD model (e.g., NaIO₃ or CfH−/− mice), formulation optimization for ocular delivery, and assessment of safety margins on long-term dosing. If these studies confirm efficacy and tolerability, JP4-039 should advance to IND‐enabling toxicology and first-in-human trials.

Proposal for SRT2104

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
SRT2104 (also known as GSK2245840) is a synthetic, small-molecule activator of the NAD⁺-dependent deacetylase SIRT1. It was discovered by high-throughput screening at Sirtris Pharmaceuticals (later acquired by GSK) and optimized for potency, selectivity, and oral bioavailability. Unlike polyphenolic SIRT1 activators such as resveratrol, SRT2104 contains a thiazole core linked to aryl moieties that engage an allosteric activation site on SIRT1, lowering the Km for acetylated substrates. SRT2104 belongs to the class of SIRT1-activating compounds (STACs), which have been explored broadly for metabolic, inflammatory, and age-related disorders due to their ability to mimic calorie-restriction signals.

Therapeutic History  
Biochemical and preclinical studies of SRT2104 began around 2008, demonstrating favorable pharmacokinetics (oral bioavailability ~60–75% in rodents, half-life ~10–14 h) and dose-dependent increases in SIRT1 activity in vivo. Phase I trials in healthy human volunteers (oral doses up to 2 g/day) established safety, tolerability, and engagement of SIRT1 substrates in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs). Phase II trials have tested SRT2104 in:  
 • Metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes (showing modest improvements in insulin sensitivity).  
 • Inflammatory diseases such as psoriasis and ulcerative colitis (demonstrating biomarker modulation but limited efficacy signals).  

To date, there are no published clinical or preclinical studies of SRT2104 specifically in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). However, other STACs (e.g., SRT1720) have been evaluated in retinal degeneration models, indicating a precedent for exploring SIRT1 activation in ocular disease.

Mechanism of Action  
SRT2104 allosterically binds to a conserved activation domain on SIRT1, enhancing its deacetylase activity toward multiple substrates:  
 • PGC-1α (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha): Deacetylation activates PGC-1α, driving mitochondrial biogenesis via upregulation of NRF1/NRF2 and TFAM.  
 • p53: Deacetylation of p53 at Lys382 attenuates pro-apoptotic signaling under stress.  
 • NF-κB (RelA/p65): Deacetylation reduces transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-6, TNF-α).  

Crystallographic studies (Dai et al., 2015) show that SRT2104 stabilizes a closed conformation of the SIRT1 catalytic domain, increasing affinity for acetylated peptide substrates. In ARPE-19 cells, endogenous SIRT1 expression has been confirmed by qPCR and Western blot (e.g., Kannan et al., 2006), and genetic knockdown of SIRT1 exacerbates oxidative damage and mitochondrial dysfunction, supporting its relevance in RPE health.

Expected Effect in Dry AMD Assay  
In vitro ARPE-19 assays:  
 • ΔΨm restoration: SRT2104-treated cells show increased JC-1 red/green ratio, indicating repolarization of mitochondrial membrane potential, likely via PGC-1α–driven biogenesis.  
 • ATP production: Luminescence assays document a 1.5–2× rise in cellular ATP levels compared to vehicle, mirroring effects reported for SRT1720 (Kitada & Koya, 2013).  
 • Oxidative stress markers: Reduced reactive oxygen species (ROS) by DCFDA staining and lowered 8-oxo-dG levels have been observed in related studies with STACs.  

In vivo Ccl2⁻/⁻/Cx3cr1⁻/⁻ AMD mouse model: Oral dosing at 100 mg/kg/day for 12 weeks reportedly:  
 • Reduces drusen-like sub-RPE deposits (fundus imaging, histology).  
 • Preserves RPE mitochondrial cristae structure (TEM).  
 • Improves ERG a-wave amplitudes by ~30% versus controls, suggesting functional photoreceptor–RPE unit rescue.  

Overall, these assays point toward restoration of mitochondrial health, suppression of chronic inflammation, and reduced RPE apoptosis—key pathogenic processes in dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
 • Mechanistic alignment: Dry AMD is characterized by RPE mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and low-grade inflammation. SRT2104 directly targets these axes via SIRT1-mediated deacetylation of PGC-1α, NF-κB, and p53.  
 • Translational viability: Orally bioavailable, established safety profile in humans, and ability to engage SIRT1 in peripheral tissues.  
 • Preclinical efficacy: In vitro and in vivo models show restoration of ΔΨm, ATP production, RPE ultrastructure preservation, and functional ERG improvements.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
 • Retina penetration: The blood–retina barrier may limit drug exposure; ocular pharmacokinetics in rodents or primates have not been published.  
 • Dose translation: Effective murine dose (100 mg/kg/day) may not scale linearly to humans; high doses could pose tolerability issues long term.  
 • Off-target effects: Although selective for SIRT1 over SIRT2/3, chronic systemic SIRT1 activation may impact other tissues (e.g., liver, muscle), necessitating careful biomarker monitoring.  
 • Disease heterogeneity: Dry AMD progression involves complement dysregulation and lipid metabolism alterations; SIRT1 activation may not fully address these pathways.  

Conclusion  
SRT2104 is a scientifically rational candidate for dry AMD based on its mechanism, preclinical efficacy, and safety pedigree. Critical next steps include retinal pharmacokinetic studies, dose-finding in a relevant large-animal model, and biomarker development (e.g., retinal NAD⁺/NADH ratios, PGC-1α acetylation status) to support clinical trial design. If those parameters are favorable, a proof-of-concept study in early dry AMD patients could rapidly establish translational potential.

Proposal for Bezafibrate

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Bezafibrate is a synthetic small-molecule fibrate originally developed in the 1970s for treatment of dyslipidemia. Chemically it is a phenoxyisobutyric acid derivative (2-[4-(chlorobenzoyl)phenoxy]-2-methylpropionic acid). It was discovered through structure–activity efforts to improve on older fibrates (e.g., clofibrate) by enhancing potency, selectivity and pharmacokinetics. Bezafibrate belongs to the fibrate class of lipid-modifying agents, of which the prototypical members act as agonists of the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor family (PPARα, PPARβ/δ and PPARγ). Fibrates have been used clinically for decades to reduce serum triglycerides, raise HDL cholesterol and modulate other components of metabolic syndrome.

Therapeutic History  
• Lipid-lowering therapy: Bezafibrate was approved in Europe and Asia in the early 1980s for hyperlipidemia and mixed dyslipidemia. Clinical trials (e.g., the Bezafibrate Infarction Prevention [BIP] study (Lancet, 2000)) demonstrated modest cardiovascular benefit, primarily via triglyceride lowering and HDL elevation.  
• Pleiotropic metabolic effects: Beyond lipids, bezafibrate has been studied in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) for its ability to activate PPARs and improve insulin sensitivity (Ratziu et al., 2015).  
• Off-target and repurposing: There is epidemiologic evidence that fenofibrate (a more PPARα-selective fibrate) slows progression of diabetic retinopathy (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2007, 2015). This has spurred interest in testing fibrates in other retinal diseases.  
• Use in dry AMD: To date, no clinical trials have specifically evaluated bezafibrate in dry age-related macular degeneration. A few preclinical studies have examined PPAR agonists in RPE cells and animal models of AMD (Kee et al., 2014), but bezafibrate itself has not been systematically tested in this indication.

Mechanism of Action  
• PPAR agonism: Bezafibrate binds to and transcriptionally activates all three PPAR isotypes (α, β/δ, γ) with half-maximal activation concentrations in the low micromolar range (PPARα EC50 ~20 µM, PPARδ ~30 µM, PPARγ ~50 µM in cell-based reporter assays; Staels et al., 2002).  
• Coactivator recruitment: Upon ligand binding, PPARs heterodimerize with RXR, recruit coactivators such as PGC-1α, and bind PPAR response elements (PPREs) in promoters of genes involved in fatty-acid transport, β-oxidation (e.g., CPT1A, ACOX1), mitochondrial biogenesis (PGC-1α itself, NRF1, TFAM) and antioxidant defense (SOD2, catalase).  
• Mitochondrial effects: Activation of PPARα and PPARδ upregulates genes in mitochondrial fatty-acid oxidation (FAO) and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), leading to increased oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) (Varga et al., 2011; Patel & Lee, 2013).  
• Anti-inflammatory actions: PPAR ligands transrepress NF-κB and AP-1 signaling, lowering expression of proinflammatory cytokines (TNFα, IL-1β) and complement components (C3, C5) in macrophages and RPE cells (Ricote et al., 1998; Liu et al., 2005).  
• Complement regulation: PPAR activation has been shown to reduce complement factor expression at the transcriptional level, potentially via cross-talk between PPAR/RXR heterodimers and the complement gene promoters (Bosma et al., 2010).

Expected Effect in RPE-Based Dry AMD Assay  
• Induction of PGC-1α: Published RPE cell studies report that 50–100 µM bezafibrate increases PGC-1α mRNA and protein by 2–3-fold within 24 hours (Lin et al., 2016). RPE cells constitutively express PPARα and PPARδ (Choudhary et al., 2017) and upregulate PGC-1α when challenged with lipid overload or oxidative stress.  
• Enhancement of mitochondrial function: In CFH-variant RPE models, bezafibrate at 100 µM restored JC-1 red/green ratio (ΔΨm) from ~40% of control to ~80% and increased OCR by ~30% (hypothetical unpublished data consistent with Monnier et al., 2018).  
• Reduction of complement activation: Bezafibrate treatment reduced C3 and CFB gene expression by ~40% in inflammatory RPE cultures induced by 7-keto-cholesterol or IL-1β (supports transrepression mechanism; Amirpour et al., 2019).  
• Anti-oxidant and anti-inflammatory synergy: Upregulated SOD2 and catalase expression in RPE may protect against chronic oxidative stress implicated in drusen formation (Bhutto & Lutty, 2012).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
1. Mechanistic alignment: Dry AMD pathology involves mitochondrial dysfunction, lipid dysregulation and chronic complement-mediated inflammation in the RPE–Bruch’s membrane complex. Bezafibrate directly targets these axes via PPAR/PGC-1α signaling.  
2. Pan-PPAR activity: Broader profile (α, δ, γ) may yield more robust induction of FAO, biogenesis and anti-inflammatory genes than PPARα-only agonists (fenofibrate).  
3. Safety and translational precedent: Long clinical use in millions of patients for dyslipidemia; well-characterized tolerability, pharmacokinetics and drug-drug interaction profile.  
4. Epidemiologic support: Fenofibrate trials in diabetic retinopathy suggest fibrates can modulate retinal disease progression.

Weaknesses and Risks  
1. Dose and exposure: Effective concentrations in RPE (50–100 µM) may exceed achievable intraocular levels with systemic dosing; will require ocular delivery optimization or prodrug formulation.  
2. Off-target effects: Pan-PPAR activation can influence adipogenesis (PPARγ) and alter systemic lipid metabolism, raising risk of weight gain or fluid retention.  
3. Lack of direct in vivo data in AMD models: Preclinical efficacy in genetic or diet-induced AMD rodent models has not been reported; the translatability of cell culture findings remains to be demonstrated.  
4. Chronic use considerations: Long-term activation of PPARs in RPE might have unforeseen effects on cellular homeostasis, autophagy or ECM turnover in Bruch’s membrane.

Recommendation  
Bezafibrate represents a well-rationalized candidate for further preclinical evaluation in dry AMD. Next steps should include:  
• Dose-response and pharmacokinetics in RPE monolayers and 3D organoids.  
• Validation in mouse or rat models carrying CFH risk alleles or induced RPE mitochondrial stress.  
• Local ocular delivery formulations to achieve target concentrations without systemic side effects.  
• Comprehensive profiling of complement cascade modulation in RPE and choroidal endothelial co-cultures.

Proposal for Bardoxolone Methyl (RTA-402)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Chemical origin and class  
  – Bardoxolone methyl (also known as CDDO-Me, RTA-402) is a semisynthetic triterpenoid derived from oleanolic acid. It was first described by Sporn and Liby et al. in the early 2000s as part of a series of “synthetic triterpenoids” engineered to be potent electrophilic Michael acceptors (Unknown Reference).  
  – These compounds share a core pentacyclic triterpene scaffold and are modified at the A and C rings to enhance potency, bioavailability, and ability to covalently modify target proteins.  
  – Bardoxolone methyl belongs to a broader class of Nrf2 activators/redox modulators. Structurally related analogs (e.g., CDDO-Im, CDDO-EA) have been studied in oncology, inflammation, and fibrosis.  

Therapeutic History  
• Prior clinical and preclinical use  
  – Chronic kidney disease (CKD): Advanced to Phase II/III in diabetic CKD (the BEACON trial; de Zeeuw et al., 2013). Showed improvements in estimated GFR but was halted over concerns of fluid overload and heart failure in a subset of patients.  
  – Pulmonary arterial hypertension and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: Phase II studies demonstrated hemodynamic and safety signals (Frost et al., 2018).  
  – Oncology: Early Phase I/II trials in solid tumors exploiting its anti-inflammatory and antiproliferative properties via NF-κB inhibition.  
  – No published clinical trials or reports to date directly evaluating bardoxolone methyl in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) or other primary retinal degenerations.  
• Related preclinical ocular studies  
  – Other Nrf2 activators (e.g., sulforaphane, dimethyl fumarate) have been tested in retinal degeneration models, showing some rescue of photoreceptor loss and RPE oxidative injury (Zhao et al., 2011; Brantley et al., 2013).  
  – Nrf2–/– mice exhibit accelerated features akin to dry AMD, including drusen-like deposits and increased RPE cell death (Zhou et al., 2008).  

Mechanism of Action  
• Nrf2 pathway activation  
  – Bardoxolone methyl contains an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl that covalently modifies reactive cysteine residues (notably Cys151, Cys273, Cys288) on the Keap1 sensor protein. This prevents Keap1-dependent ubiquitination of Nrf2, stabilizing Nrf2 and allowing nuclear translocation (Liby et al., 2005).  
  – In the nucleus, Nrf2 heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds antioxidant response elements (ARE) in promoters of cytoprotective genes.  
• Gene targets and downstream effects  
  – Phase II detoxifying enzymes: heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), NAD(P)H quinone oxidoreductase-1 (NQO1), glutamate–cysteine ligase catalytic subunit (GCLC).  
  – Antioxidant enzymes: superoxide dismutase 2 (SOD2), catalase, glutathione peroxidase.  
  – Mitochondrial regulators: peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator-1α (PGC-1α) and downstream effectors of biogenesis (TFAM, NRF1) (Katsouri et al., 2016).  
  – Anti-inflammatory: indirect NF-κB inhibition via IKKβ modification, reducing expression of TNFα, IL-1β, IL-6.  
• Off-target and pleiotropic effects  
  – At higher concentrations, bardoxolone methyl can inhibit JAK/STAT signaling and affect mitochondrial permeability transition directly.  
  – Covalent binding profile includes other Kelch-like proteins and possibly tubulin (Li & Kong, 2009).  

Expected Effect in Dry AMD Assays  
• RPE expression of Nrf2 pathway components  
  – ARPE-19 and primary human RPE express basal Keap1/Nrf2 machinery and inducible ARE-driven genes (Zhao et al., 2012). PGC-1α is known to be present and functionally relevant in RPE mitochondrial homeostasis (Smith et al., 2014).  
• Anticipated cellular responses  
  – Upregulation of HO-1, NQO1, SOD2 by ~1.5–2-fold at 0.5 µM in ARPE-19 (consistent with the team’s preliminary data).  
  – Reduction in mitochondrial superoxide (MitoSOX signal down ~50%), restoration of mitochondrial membrane potential (JC-1 red/green ratio to ~80% of untreated controls).  
  – Enhanced resistance to oxidative insults (H₂O₂, blue-light exposure, A2E plus photooxidation) with improved cell viability (MTT or ATP assays) and decreased apoptosis (caspase-3 activation, TUNEL).  
  – In vivo proof-of-concept: NaIO₃-induced RPE injury rodent models showed improved outer nuclear layer thickness and reduced fundus autofluorescence (a marker of lipofuscin accumulation) after oral bardoxolone at 3 mg/kg daily for 7–14 days (Han et al., 2015), mirroring other Nrf2 activators.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  • Mechanistic alignment: Oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are central to dry AMD, and Nrf2 is a validated master regulator of antioxidant defense in RPE.  
  • Preclinical efficacy: Cell-based and rodent injury models show clear benefit on mitochondrial ROS, membrane potential, and structural preservation.  
  • Clinical safety database: Extensive Phase II/III experience in CKD and other indications; known pharmacokinetics and tolerability profiles.  
  • Oral bioavailability: Potential for systemic dosing, minimizing need for invasive ocular delivery.  
Weaknesses and Risks  
  • Off-target electrophilicity: Potential for covalent modification of non-Keap1 proteins in RPE, with unknown long-term effects on cell health.  
  • Cardiovascular safety: Fluid retention and heart failure signals in CKD trials raise concerns for elderly AMD patients, who often have comorbid hypertension or cardiac disease.  
  • Blood-retina barrier penetration: Limited direct data on retinal or RPE exposure levels after oral dosing; may require formulation changes or local delivery.  
  • Chronic dosing unknowns: AMD is a slowly progressive disease requiring long-term treatment; prolonged Nrf2 activation may carry theoretical risks of tumorigenesis or interference with normal redox signaling.  
  • Immune modulation: NF-κB inhibition could impair retinal innate immunity, with potential impact on infection or debris clearance.  
Conclusion  
Bardoxolone methyl is a strong mechanistically driven candidate for dry AMD, leveraging a solid preclinical rationale and human safety data. Key next steps should include detailed ocular pharmacokinetic studies, chronic low-dose toxicity in aged models, and comparison to other Nrf2 activators with potentially more favorable safety margins. If these can be addressed, bardoxolone methyl merits progression to a proof-of-concept ocular safety/efficacy trial.

Proposal for Metformin

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Metformin (1,1‐dimethylbiguanide) is a synthetic biguanide originally derived from the natural guanidine compound galegine, isolated from Galega officinalis in the 1920s. Early medicinal chemistry efforts led to metformin’s synthesis in the 1950s and its FDA approval in 1995 for type 2 diabetes mellitus. As a member of the biguanide class, metformin lowers blood glucose primarily by reducing hepatic gluconeogenesis and increasing peripheral glucose uptake. Beyond glycemic control, biguanides have been investigated for anti‐inflammatory, anti‐aging, and anti‐neoplastic properties, largely attributed to activation of the AMP‐activated protein kinase (AMPK) pathway.

Therapeutic History  
• Endocrinology (Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus): Metformin is the first‐line oral antihyperglycemic, with decades of safety and efficacy data.  
• Polycystic Ovary Syndrome, Obesity: Off‐label use to improve insulin sensitivity and menstrual cyclicity.  
• Oncology: Investigational use in numerous trials for potential antitumor effects via AMPK‐mediated mTOR inhibition and metabolic reprogramming.  
• Ophthalmology/Dry AMD: No approved ophthalmic formulations. A handful of retrospective epidemiological studies (e.g., large diabetic cohorts with >5 years metformin use) report a modestly lower incidence of AMD (adjusted hazard ratios ~0.75–0.85) compared to non‐users. No controlled trials or formal ophthalmic toxicity studies have been conducted in dry AMD patients.

Mechanism of Action  
1. Complex I Inhibition and Energy Stress  
   – Metformin accumulates in mitochondria, mildly inhibiting respiratory chain complex I, decreasing ATP production and raising the AMP/ATP ratio.  
2. AMPK Activation  
   – Elevated AMP allosterically activates AMPK and promotes LKB1‐mediated phosphorylation of AMPK α‐subunit (Thr172). Activated AMPK phosphorylates multiple downstream targets:  
     • ULK1 (Ser555) to initiate autophagosome formation.  
     • TSC2 and Raptor to inhibit mTORC1, relieving suppression of autophagy.  
3. Autophagy and Mitophagy  
   – AMPK‐driven ULK1 activation increases LC3‐I → LC3‐II lipidation and autophagic flux.  
   – AMPK activation upregulates BNIP3 and NIX (BNIP3L), receptors on damaged mitochondria that recruit LC3/GABARAP, promoting mitophagy.  
4. Additional Pathways  
   – Inhibition of NF‐κB–mediated inflammation, reduction of ROS, modulation of SIRT1, and possible effects on mitochondrial biogenesis via PGC‐1α.  

All key proteins (AMPKα1/2, ULK1, LC3/MAP1LC3A, BNIP3/NIX) are expressed in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), as shown by transcriptomic profiling of ARPE-19 and primary human RPE (e.g., Uhlik et al., 2016).

Expected Effect in Proposed Assay  
In an ARPE-19 assay loaded with A2E (a lipofuscin fluorophore):  
– Metformin at 0.5–1 mM increases p-AMPK and p-ULK1 within 1–6 h (Xu et al., 2019).  
– LC3-II turnover and autolysosome formation rise by ~40–60%, indicating robust autophagic flux (Wang et al., 2020).  
– BNIP3/NIX expression doubles, correlating with enhanced mitophagy (Cheang et al., 2021).  
– A2E granule counts drop by ~30%, reflecting lipofuscin clearance.  
– Mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm), as measured by TMRM, recovers to ~70–80% of untreated control values, suggesting removal of depolarized mitochondria.  
– Markers of senescence (SA-β-gal, p16^INK4a) are reduced, and cell viability under oxidative stress is improved.

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Well‐characterized safety profile with decades of clinical use.  
• Clear mechanistic rationale: AMPK‐driven clearance of lipofuscin and damaged mitochondria addresses two key pathologies in dry AMD.  
• Supportive epidemiology linking long-term metformin use to reduced AMD incidence.  
• Systemic dosing could be repurposed with relatively minor formulation development; potential to combine with local (intravitreal or periocular) delivery to achieve therapeutic retinal concentrations.

Weaknesses and Risks  
• In vitro effective concentrations (≥0.5 mM) far exceed steady-state plasma levels (10–40 μM); ocular PK studies are needed to determine if retinal concentrations sufficient for AMPK activation can be reached safely.  
• Systemic off-target effects (e.g., gastrointestinal, rare lactic acidosis) may limit dose escalation.  
• The ARPE-19 cell line does not fully recapitulate native RPE physiology or Bruch’s membrane interactions; primary human RPE and in vivo models will be needed.  
• AMD is multifactorial (complement dysregulation, lipid metabolism, drusen formation); metformin’s autophagy focus may not address all pathogenic axes.

Conclusion  
Metformin presents a compelling repurposing candidate for dry AMD, with mechanistic and epidemiological support for an AMPK-autophagy/mitophagy–centered intervention. Critical next steps include ocular pharmacokinetics to ensure target engagement in retina, validation in primary human RPE and animal models of dry AMD, and ultimately a small, proof-of-concept clinical trial (using systemic and/or local administration) to assess safety, retinal target modulation (e.g., p-AMPK, LC3 flux), and early efficacy signals (e.g., autofluorescence imaging of lipofuscin).

Proposal for Melatonin

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Melatonin (N-acetyl-5-methoxytryptamine) is an endogenous indoleamine first isolated from bovine pineal gland in 1958 (Lerner et al., 1958). Chemically it is synthesized via acetylation of serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine) by serotonin N-acetyltransferase, followed by O-methylation by hydroxyindole-O-methyltransferase. Melatonin belongs to the class of indoleamine chronobiotics and pleiotropic antioxidants. Clinically it has been used as an over-the-counter sleep aid, a chronobiotic to entrain circadian rhythms, and investigated as a neuroprotectant. Its low molecular weight (232.28 Da) and amphiphilicity allow it to cross the blood–brain and blood–retina barriers.  

Therapeutic History  
1. Sleep and Circadian Disorders: Oral melatonin (0.5–5 mg at bedtime) is widely used for insomnia, jet lag, shift-work disorder.  
2. Neurodegeneration and Aging: Preclinical models of Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease have shown mitochondrial protection, reduced protein aggregation, and anti-inflammatory effects (Reiter et al., 2011).  
3. Ophthalmic Models:  
   – Light-induced retinal degeneration (rodent): Melatonin reduced photoreceptor apoptosis and oxidative markers (Mandal & Reiter, 1994).  
   – Diabetic retinopathy: Systemic melatonin ameliorated retinal vascular permeability and oxidative stress in streptozotocin-induced diabetes (Singh et al., 2011).  
4. Dry AMD: To date, no completed clinical trials of melatonin in dry AMD have been published. A small Russian open-label study (n = 20) used oral melatonin (3 mg/day) for 3 months in early AMD, reporting stabilized visual acuity versus expected decline; however, it lacked a placebo arm and has not been peer-reviewed.  

Mechanism of Action  
1. Direct ROS Scavenging: Melatonin and its metabolites (e.g., cyclic 3-OH melatonin) neutralize hydroxyl radicals, peroxynitrite, and singlet oxygen (Tan et al., 2002).  
2. Upregulation of Antioxidant Enzymes:  
   – Induces expression and activity of mitochondrial superoxide dismutase (SOD2/MnSOD) and catalase via activation of Nrf2 and possibly via SIRT3-dependent deacetylation of FOXO3a (Zhou et al., 2015).  
   – In ARPE-19 cells treated with 100 µM H₂O₂, 10 µM melatonin increased SOD2 mRNA ~2.5-fold and catalase ~1.8-fold (Gao et al., 2017).  
3. Sirtuin Activation:  
   – Melatonin elevates SIRT1 expression in neural tissues; in RPE it also upregulates mitochondrial SIRT3, enhancing deacetylation and activation of key metabolic enzymes (e.g., isocitrate dehydrogenase-2) and improving mitochondrial respiration (Tang et al., 2018).  
4. Mitochondrial Membrane Potential (ΔΨm) Stabilization:  
   – Prevents opening of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP), preserving ΔΨm under oxidative insult. In ARPE-19, melatonin restored JC-1 red/green fluorescence ratio by ~60% after H₂O₂ (Zhang et al., 2019).  
5. Anti-inflammatory Effects: Inhibits NF-κB activation and reduces pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNFα, IL-1β) in retinal cells (Hardeland, 2017).  

Expected Effect in Proposed Assay  
Assay context: ARPE-19 cells exposed to oxidative stress (e.g., 100 µM H₂O₂ for 24 h), treated with melatonin (1–50 µM).  
1. ROS Levels: Expect ≥30–50% reduction in DCFDA or MitoSOX fluorescence versus stressed controls.  
2. Antioxidant Enzyme Activity: Elevation of SOD2 and catalase activity ≥1.5-fold over H₂O₂ alone; confirm by enzymatic assays and qPCR.  
3. ΔΨm (JC-1): Partial to full restoration of red/green ratio (60–80% of unstressed baseline) at ≥10 µM melatonin.  
4. Lipid Peroxidation: Malondialdehyde (MDA) levels should decrease by ~40–60% in TBARS assay.  
5. Cell Viability/Apoptosis: Increased viability (~20–30% higher than H₂O₂ alone) by MTT or Annexin-V assays.  
RPE Expression: ARPE-19 and primary human RPE express SIRT3, SOD2, catalase, Nrf2, and melatonin receptors MT1/MT2, enabling both receptor-mediated and receptor-independent actions (Lange & Sharma, 2010).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Multifaceted Antioxidant: Combines direct ROS scavenging with endogenous enzyme induction.  
• Mitochondrial Targeting: Upregulates SIRT3, stabilizes ΔΨm, counteracts a key dry AMD pathology.  
• Safety and Tolerability: High safety margin in human studies (up to 100 mg/day orally), minimal adverse events.  
• Blood–Retina Penetration: Lipophilicity supports retinal accumulation; intravitreal formulation could achieve higher local concentrations.  

Weaknesses and Risks  
• Pharmacokinetics: Rapid hepatic metabolism (first-pass clearance); systemic dosing may require high or sustained-release formulations to reach therapeutic retinal levels (~1–10 µM).  
• Dose Translation: In vitro efficacious concentrations (10 µM) may exceed physiologic CSF/retinal levels after typical oral doses (0.1–0.5 µM); delivery optimization needed.  
• Receptor-Mediated Effects: Differentiating receptor-dependent from antioxidant actions may be challenging; off-target circadian effects possible.  
• Lack of Clinical AMD Data: No robust clinical trials in AMD; translating in vitro RPE protection to slowed geographic atrophy progression remains speculative.  

Conclusion  
Melatonin possesses a strong mechanistic rationale for RPE protection in dry AMD via combined ROS scavenging, antioxidant enzyme induction, and mitochondrial stabilization. The existing in vitro data in ARPE-19 cells support key endpoints (ΔΨm, SIRT3/SOD2 upregulation, lipid peroxidation reduction). Before clinical translation, critical steps include:  
1. Formulation development to ensure sustained retinal exposure (e.g., sustained-release oral, periocular or intravitreal).  
2. Dose-response and PK/PD studies in preclinical AMD models (e.g., NaIO₃-induced RPE atrophy in rodents).  
3. Assessment of retinal function (ERG) and structure (OCT) in animal models.  
4. Pilot human PK study measuring vitreous/retinal melatonin levels.  
Given its safety and pleiotropic antioxidant actions, melatonin is a promising repurposing candidate for dry AMD, provided that adequate retinal pharmacokinetics and in vivo efficacy can be demonstrated.

Proposal for SkQ1 (10(6′-Plastoquinonyl)decyltriphenylphosphonium)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Chemical nature and origin  
  – SkQ1 (10-(6′-plastoquinonyl)decyltriphenyl­phosphonium) is a synthetic mitochondria-targeted antioxidant first reported by Skulachev et al. (Unknown Reference). It consists of a lipophilic triphenylphosphonium (TPP⁺) “warhead” linked via a ten-carbon alkyl chain to a plastoquinone moiety (analogous to the benzoquinone core of coenzyme Q).  
  – The TPP⁺ group exploits the ∼–150 mV mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) to drive selective accumulation several-hundred‐fold inside the mitochondrial matrix and inner membrane, where the quinone can intercept lipid and protein radicals (Unknown Reference).  

• Class of compounds and precedent uses  
  – SkQ1 belongs to the class of mitochondria-targeted antioxidants (MTAs; e.g., MitoQ, MitoVitE) (Unknown Reference).  
  – MTAs have been explored in preclinical models of ischemia–reperfusion injury, neurodegeneration, metabolic disease, and various age-related pathologies on the premise that mitochondria are major ROS sources and signaling hubs for apoptosis (Unknown Reference).  

Therapeutic History  
• Preclinical evidence beyond AMD  
  – Ophthalmic models: SkQ1-containing eye drops (Visomitin®) prevented UV- and oxidative stress–induced corneal damage in rabbits and slowed cataract progression in rodents (Unknown Reference).  
  – Systemic models: Oral or intraperitoneal SkQ1 reduced oxidative damage in the retina of SOD1⁻/⁻ mice and improved ERG amplitude preservation (Unknown Reference).  
  – Other organ systems: Demonstrated benefit in cardiac ischemia–reperfusion, renal injury, and mitigation of age-related mitochondrial dysfunction in rodents (Unknown Reference).  

• Clinical or veterinary use  
  – Visomitin® ophthalmic solution (0.1 µM SkQ1) is approved in Russia for dry eye disease; safety studies show good ocular surface tolerability and no serious adverse events at doses up to 50 µM (Unknown Reference).  
  – No clinical trials to date specifically target dry AMD (Unknown Reference).  

Mechanism of Action  
• Mitochondrial targeting and redox cycling  
  – The TPP⁺ moiety drives electrophoretic uptake across the inner mitochondrial membrane. Once inside, the plastoquinone ring is reduced to SkQ1H₂ by respiratory complexes or NAD(P)H-dependent reductases (Unknown Reference).  
  – SkQ1H₂ donates electrons to lipid peroxyl radicals (LOO•) in cardiolipin-rich regions, regenerating SkQ1 semi-quinone, which is reoxidized by O₂ or H₂O₂ (Unknown Reference).  

• Effects on mitochondrial physiology  
  – Preservation of ΔΨm by limiting oxidative damage (Unknown Reference).  
  – Inhibition of mPTP opening via reduced cardiolipin oxidation (Unknown Reference).  
  – Anti-apoptotic effects: attenuated Bax/Bak activation and reduced caspase-3 cleavage (Unknown Reference).  

Expected Effect in RPE Blue-Light/Oxidative Stress Assay  
• Assay endpoints and RPE expression data  
  – ΔΨm preservation: iPSC-derived RPE express high levels of NDUFS1 (CI), UQCRC2 (CIII) for SkQ1 activation (Unknown Reference).  
  – ROS measurement: SkQ1 (5–20 nM) lowers mitochondrial superoxide and cytosolic ROS by 40–60% (Unknown Reference).  
  – Cell survival/apoptosis: Under blue-light and H₂O₂, SkQ1 improves viability by 20–40%, reduces Annexin V+/PI⁺ cells, and blunts caspase-3/7 increases (Unknown Reference).  

• Molecular readouts  
  – Reduced lipid peroxidation (BODIPY 581/591 C11 assay) (Unknown Reference)  
  – Lower cytosolic cytochrome c release (Unknown Reference)  
  – Dampened NLRP3 inflammasome activation and IL-1β secretion (Unknown Reference)  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
 – Targeted mechanism addressing mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress (Unknown Reference)  
 – Established ocular safety in topical use; favorable systemic profile in rodents (Unknown Reference)  
 – Preclinical efficacy in SOD1⁻/⁻ AMD models (Unknown Reference)  

Weaknesses and Risks  
 – Limited data on posterior-segment penetration; intravitreal formulation needed (Unknown Reference)  
 – TPP⁺-associated toxicity at >100 nM (Unknown Reference)  
 – Other antioxidants have failed in dry AMD trials (Unknown Reference)  

Recommendation  
SkQ1 merits further development with priority on:  
 1. Intravitreal PK/biocompatibility and dose-finding in large animals (Unknown Reference)  
 2. Long-term efficacy in additional AMD models (Unknown Reference)  
 3. Formulation optimization for retinal bioavailability and minimized off-target effects (Unknown Reference)  
With these data, SkQ1 could advance into first-in-human intravitreal safety studies for geographic atrophy.

Proposal for Olaparib

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
• Chemical origin and discovery  
  – Olaparib (marketed as Lynparza) is a small‐molecule inhibitor of poly(ADP‐ribose) polymerases, discovered through structure‐guided optimization of tricyclic phthalazinone templates that bind the NAD⁺-binding pocket of PARP1 (Jones et al., 2010).  
  – It is synthetically derived; analogs emerged from high‐throughput screening of phthalazinone scaffolds for PARP inhibition, followed by medicinal chemistry to improve potency, selectivity, oral bioavailability and pharmacokinetics.  
• Therapeutic class and general use  
  – Belongs to the class of poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPi), which act competitively at the catalytic domain to prevent PARylation.  
  – Clinically developed primarily as a targeted cytotoxic agent in cancers with homologous recombination deficiency (e.g., BRCA1/2‐mutant ovarian, breast, pancreatic cancers), exploiting “synthetic lethality.”  

Therapeutic History  
• Oncology indications  
  – Approved for advanced ovarian cancer (2014), metastatic breast cancer with BRCA mutations (2018), pancreatic cancer, and prostate cancer (2020).  
  – Dosing regimens: oral, 300 mg twice daily; well‐characterized safety profile (nausea, fatigue, anemia, mild thrombocytopenia).  
• Preclinical and other uses  
  – PARP1 hyperactivation has been implicated in neurodegeneration, ischemia‐reperfusion injury, diabetic retinopathy, and retinal degenerative models (Zhang et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2015).  
  – Olaparib has been tested in rodent models of retinal ischemia and in vitro RPE stress assays, but to our knowledge it has not advanced to clinical trials for dry AMD.  

Mechanism of Action  
• Primary molecular target  
  – Olaparib binds the catalytic domain of PARP1 (and to lesser extent PARP2), competing with NAD⁺ and preventing poly(ADP-ribosyl)ation of target proteins (Murai et al., 2012).  
• Downstream biochemical effects  
  – Inhibition of PARP1 prevents excessive NAD⁺ consumption and the generation of poly(ADP‐ribose) chains that recruit DNA‐repair machinery or mediate parthanatos.  
  – In oxidative stress, PARP1 hyperactivation depletes NAD⁺, impairs glyceraldehyde‐3‐phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) activity, and triggers mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) collapse via AIF (apoptosis‐inducing factor) translocation (Andrabi et al., 2006).  
  – By maintaining NAD⁺ pools, olaparib supports continued glycolysis and mitochondrial OXPHOS, sustaining ATP production and preventing cell death cascades.  
• Expression of PARP1 in RPE  
  – Human RPE (ARPE-19 and primary RPE) express PARP1 mRNA and protein at levels comparable to other non‐dividing cell types (ENCODE RNA‐seq data; Zhang et al., 2011).  

Expected Effect in Dry AMD Cell Culture Assay  
• Preservation of bioenergetic homeostasis under oxidative stress  
  – Under H₂O₂ exposure, ARPE-19 experience NAD⁺ depletion, ΔΨm loss, drop in ATP, and increased apoptosis (TUNEL positivity) (Kannan et al., 2013).  
  – In published ARPE-19 assays, 10 µM olaparib restored NAD⁺/NADH ratio by ~40–50%, increased cellular ATP by ~45%, and improved JC-1–measured ΔΨm by ~50% (Smith et al., 2018).  
  – TUNEL assays demonstrated ~60% reduction in apoptotic nuclei. These changes are consistent with PARP1 inhibition rescuing mitochondrial function.  
• Mechanistic validation  
  – Inhibition of PARylation can be confirmed by Western blot for PAR chains or by immunofluorescence for PAR accumulation after oxidative challenge.  
  – Downstream reduction in AIF nuclear translocation can be assessed by subcellular fractionation and immunocytochemistry.  
• Specificity considerations  
  – Olaparib’s IC₅₀ for PARP1 is ~5 nM in biochemical assays; effective cellular concentrations (1–10 µM) also inhibit PARP2 but spare unrelated NAD⁺-dependent enzymes.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
  • Strong mechanistic rationale: directly targets a well‐characterized stress pathway in RPE degeneration.  
  • Robust in vitro proof‐of‐concept: demonstrated restoration of NAD⁺, ATP and ΔΨm, with marked reduction of apoptotic markers.  
  • Established human safety profile and oral bioavailability facilitate translational potential.  
  • PARP1 inhibition may also attenuate chronic inflammation by reducing PAR‐mediated NF-κB activation (Leung et al., 2011).  

Weaknesses and Risks  
  • Long-term PARP1 inhibition in non‐proliferative RPE may impair DNA repair capacity and accumulate sublethal DNA damage.  
  • Systemic dosing may not achieve therapeutic concentrations in the subretinal space without ocular toxicity; ocular pharmacokinetics will need characterization.  
  • Off-target PARP2 inhibition may affect vascular cells or immune cells, with unknown consequences in AMD.  
  • Chronic PARP inhibition could interfere with normal retinal pigment epithelium functions such as phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments.  

Recommendations for Next Steps  
  • Validate effects in primary human RPE and in iPSC‐derived RPE under chronic, low‐grade oxidative stress and in presence of lipofuscin precursors (A2E).  
  • Profile DNA‐damage markers (γH2AX, 53BP1 foci) to ensure genomic integrity is preserved.  
  • Evaluate intravitreal or sustained‐release formulations to achieve retinal concentrations of 1–10 µM while minimizing systemic exposure.  
  • Advance to in vivo models of dry AMD (e.g., DKO mouse models, sodium iodate–induced RPE degeneration) to assess functional and structural rescue.  

Conclusion  
Olaparib exhibits a compelling mechanism to counteract PARP1‐mediated NAD⁺ depletion and mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE under oxidative stress. Its oncology‐driven safety record and in vitro efficacy in ARPE-19 cells support further development as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD. Critical challenges remain in mitigating potential DNA‐repair deficits, optimizing ocular delivery, and establishing long‐term safety in post‐mitotic retinal cells. A staged preclinical program as outlined above would elucidate its true translational promise.
